docs.title: Traffic Monitor docs
docs.text:
Traffic Monitor is open source software that turns a Raspberry Pi 5 with a camera and a Doppler radar into a roadway counter and speed monitor. It counts pedestrians, bicycles, and vehicles, measures vehicle speeds, and keeps the data on the device.

Be counted

Privacy is part of the design. Object detection runs on the device, the database records labels, speeds, and times rather than people, and nothing is sent to an outside server unless you set it up. Data and privacy lists what the device stores, including the short-lived snapshots and clips that Frigate keeps by default, and who on your network can see them.

Our mission is to democratize the power of AI tools to improve community safety and quality of life, through the ethical and transparent use of these capabilities.

docs.title: Choose a site and mount
docs.text:
Deployment covers where the device goes, how it's mounted, and the angle of the camera and radar to the roadway. The zones and location are set afterwards in First-time setup.

Danger

Follow the law. Comply with all applicable laws and local regulations when installing, mounting, and deploying a Traffic Monitor, particularly in public spaces. Unauthorized surveillance can lead to legal consequences and infringe privacy rights. Consult legal professionals or local authorities if you are unsure of the requirements. This guide is for educational purposes; you are responsible for complying with the law and for the consequences of deploying and using the device.

Mount the device only where you have permission, and don't attach it to utility poles without proper authorization.

docs.title: Mounting options
docs.text:
Choose a mount that lets you make fine adjustments, because the radar's angle and position need tuning on site.

The open source, 3D-printed enclosure has several mounting methods built in, depending on the variant:

  • 1/4"-20 screw insert on the bottom and back, for camera and trail-camera mounting hardware
  • VESA-compatible holes (75 and 100 mm)
  • Arca-Swiss-compatible quick-release plate on the bottom, for tripods
  • Strap slots on the back, for posts, poles, and trees
  • Safety tether hole for a carabiner and strap
Back: VESA holes, 1/4"-20 screw insert, strap slots, and safety tether hole (lower left) Bottom: Arca-Swiss quick-release plate and 1/4"-20 screw insert

docs.title: Temporary deployments
docs.text:
For counts over a few hours, such as an event or a point-in-time study, mount the device at or above head height with an unobstructed view of the roadway. A sturdy tripod and a compact portable power station work well.

On a 16-foot telescoping tripod, counting event participants Recording manual confirmation counts, with the device on a camera tripod and a portable power station

docs.title: Permanent deployments
docs.text:
Warning

Work safely. Use proper safety equipment and ladder practice. Make sure the device is securely mounted, all fasteners are tight, the safety tether is in place, and the mount is stable. Failure to do so can cause injury or property damage.

Long-term deployments work anywhere the camera has a good view of the roadway and the radar can be aimed along it: garage roofs, a wood post in a cement-filled bucket, a stone pillar. Keep the device out of reach and clear of anything that might grow or be parked in front of it.

Long-term deployments, with permission, on a private rooftop and a gate entrance

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Mount the device above the roadway and out of reach, about 10 to 12 feet up, for the best view and the least tampering.
  • Choose a clear view of the road. Objects are still tracked when they pass briefly behind a tree or lamp post.
  • Keep the radar off parking spots and other places where vehicles stop, because stationary vehicles get in the way of its readings.
  • The camera detects objects anywhere in its field of view, so frame the whole stretch of road you care about.
  • Think about which zones your use case needs, and whether the view lets you draw them.

docs.title: Camera considerations
docs.text:
The camera detects objects anywhere in the frame, so cover the whole area of interest even if the roadway isn't centered. An unobstructed view gives the best results.

Detections can happen anywhere in the camera's field of view

docs.title: Radar considerations
docs.text:
The radar has a narrower field of view than the camera and measures speed accurately only at a shallow angle to the direction of travel.

  • Aim the device so that traffic moves toward or away from it at 45 degrees or less. The OmniPreSense field-of-view calculator shows how the angle affects the reading.
  • The radar labels movement inbound (toward the device) and outbound (away from it), and the camera uses the same words. Place the device so those directions make sense for your roadway, for example inbound for downhill traffic.
  • To find the radar's coverage, have someone hold the radar outside the case and watch the red and blue LEDs on its front as people and vehicles pass. Where the LEDs blink is where to draw zone_radar.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: Plug the device in. It starts by itself, and the green LED on the Raspberry Pi shows it has power. Continue with First-time setup.

docs.title: 1. Get a Traffic Monitor
docs.text:
• Build your own

    Buy the hardware, assemble it, and install the software. The software is open source and the parts are sold at retail.

  • Start with a pre-built unit

    The software is installed. Skip to step 2, and ask your provider how the unit connects to your network.

docs.title: 2. Deploy it
docs.text: The device needs a clear view of the roadway, and the radar needs a shallow angle to the direction of travel. Choose a site and mount covers both, for temporary and permanent deployments.

docs.title: 3. Set it up
docs.text: Power it on and follow First-time setup: open the home page, turn on detection, adjust the zones to your roadway, and record the device's location. This takes about half an hour.

docs.title: 4. Use the data
docs.text:
The device counts around the clock and starts again by itself after a power cut. Watch the Monitoring dashboard, review detections in Frigate, export the data, or send it to ThingsBoard.

Some operators pair the device with a display that shows the day's counts. Share what you build in Show and tell or on the Zulip chat.

LED display showing daily counts from a Traffic Monitor

docs.title: First-time setup
docs.text:
Do these steps once the device is mounted and powered on, and again whenever you move it. You need a computer or phone on the same network or on the device's own hotspot, and the device's setup code or administrator login. A device without a radar also needs an SSH client for step 4.

As installed, the camera and the first radar are turned on in the Traffic Monitor's settings, but Frigate's object detection is off. Nothing is counted until you turn it on in step 2.

docs.title: 1. Claim the device
docs.text:
Open http://<device>/, where <device> is the hostname you set when imaging the card followed by .local, or the device's IP address. Home page and apps explains each link and how to find the address.

A device at the roadside has no network to join. If its Wi-Fi isn't on a network it knows, it runs its own hotspot, named TM- and four characters. Join it with the password from the device's card; your phone's sign-in window then opens the setup page by itself, or you can open http://10.42.0.1/. Wi-Fi and the hotspot has the details, including what to do on an iPhone or an Android 17 phone.

A device that hasn't been claimed opens its setup page:

  1. Choose Start setup, and read and accept the license agreement.
  2. Enter the setup code from the end of the installer's output, or from the card that came with a pre-built unit. sudo tm-control card on the device shows it again.
  3. Create the administrator account with a username and password, and choose Claim this device.
  4. Optionally, set a new system password for Cockpit and SSH.

Control app and login explains each step, and how to add accounts for other people. If the device was claimed already, log in as the administrator.

docs.title: 2. Turn on detection
docs.text:
1. Open Frigate from the home page, logged in as the administrator.
  2. Go to Settings > Configuration editor.
  3. Under cameras: picam_h265: detect:, change enabled: false to enabled: true.
  4. Choose Save & Restart.

When Frigate is back, its live view draws a box around anything that moves past the camera.

docs.title: 3. Adjust the zones
docs.text:
The Traffic Monitor looks for four zones with fixed names. Frigate ships with all four drawn for a sample roadway; drag their corners to fit yours.

  1. In Frigate, go to Settings > Camera configuration > Masks / Zones.
  2. Edit each zone in the table below, then save. Frigate restarts.
Zone Draw it over Used for zone_capture The whole roadway you want to count, including sidewalks that are clearly in view Counting. An object is counted only if it passes through this zone. zone_near The half of zone_capture closest to the device Direction zone_far The half of zone_capture farthest from the device Direction. An object that enters zone_near and then zone_far is moving outbound, away from the device; the reverse is inbound. zone_radar The part of the road the radar covers accurately, roughly a rectangle from curb to curb in the middle of the frame. Skip it if the device has no radar. Speed statistics. Any object that enters a zone gets a speed from the radar, but the dashboards' speed statistics use only objects that passed through this zone. Radar considerations shows how to find the radar's coverage. The four zones drawn over a residential street

Zones you draw for your own analysis, such as a stop-sign zone or a crosswalk, can have any other name. Ideas and use cases has examples.

docs.title: 4. Record the location and sensors
docs.text:
The location is optional. If the device stays in one place and you never share its data, it can count without one. To record where the device is and which way it faces:

  1. Open Location from the control app's menu, as the administrator.
  2. Choose Add a place. Enter a description that only you see, paste the latitude and longitude from any maps app, and choose the way each sensor faces. Choose Save.
  3. Open the new place in the list, choose Deploy here, check the review, and choose Deploy.

To record only the way the sensors face, choose Modify deployment on the place in use, First location, and change the bearings there. Places and location explains each step, and how precisely the database stores the location.

Then check that the sensors in the Traffic Monitor's settings match the hardware. A device with the Pi camera and one radar needs no change. A device without a radar needs enabled: false under TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00. Connect over SSH and open the settings file:

sudo nano /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml

The camera and radar, as installed:

sensors:
    cameras:
        picam_h265:
            enabled: true
            camera_radar: TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00
    radars:
        TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00:
            enabled: true

Save with Ctrl+O and leave nano with Ctrl+X. The Traffic Monitor reads the file again as soon as you save it, so no restart is needed. A change that doesn't take effect usually means a YAML error, such as a wrong indent.

config.yml settings describes every setting in this file, including the optional ThingsBoard upload.

docs.title: 5. Check the counts
docs.text:
Open Dashboard from the home page and choose Monitoring in the sidebar. Monitoring shows a count a few seconds after each object passes through zone_capture, and speed statistics for objects that also passed through zone_radar. Today's counts start at 04:00 local time, so between midnight and 04:00 they're empty.

No counts?

Work down the list:

  1. Frigate shows no boxes around moving objects. Detection is off (step 2), or the camera is off: in the configuration editor, cameras: picam_h265: needs enabled: true. If the live view is black, open Camera feeds from the home page to check that the camera itself streams.
  2. Frigate detects objects, but the dashboard stays at zero. The objects aren't passing through zone_capture (step 3), or the camera is off in the Traffic Monitor's settings: sensors: cameras: picam_h265: needs enabled: true, and the name must match Frigate's camera name. If your edits don't take effect, check the file for a YAML error.
  3. Counts but no speeds. The radar must be enabled: true and named in the camera's camera_radar, zone_radar must cover the road, and the radar must have been plugged in when the software was installed. If you added it later, rerun bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm.
  4. Still nothing. Look at the logs in System administration, then ask in the chat.

docs.title: Install the software
docs.text: The Traffic Monitor runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 with Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit). One installer script sets up the operating system, detects the radars and the AI accelerator, builds the containers on the device, and reboots when it needs to.

docs.title: Prepare the card
docs.text:
1. Open Raspberry Pi Imager on your computer, with the microSD card in a card reader.
  2. Choose Raspberry Pi OS (other) > Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit). The full desktop image works but installs software the Traffic Monitor doesn't use.
  3. In OS customization, set a hostname, a username and password, your Wi-Fi network, and turn on SSH. The hostname becomes the device's address on your network: http://<hostname>.local/.
  4. Write the card, put it in the Raspberry Pi, and power it on. The first boot takes a few minutes.

docs.title: Install on the device
docs.text:
The device needs an internet connection during the install. Afterwards it runs offline.

Connect over SSH with the username and hostname you chose:

ssh <username>@<hostname>.local

Then download the repository and run the installer:

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y git
git clone https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor
bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh

The installer asks for your password when it needs administrator rights. If the device has no Wi-Fi country yet, it also asks for one, as a two-letter code such as US or GB, because the device's hotspot needs it; press Enter for US. A first install takes 30 minutes or more. Building Frigate's container image compiles ffmpeg on the device, which alone takes about 20 minutes with little output, so leave it running.

Near the end, the installer shows the device's card on the terminal: its setup code, which you need once to claim the device and create its administrator account, and the name and password of its hotspot. Keep them; the hotspot's password isn't in the installer's log, and sudo tm-control card prints the card again. Control app and login says where else to find the setup code.

Then the installer asks to reboot. A first install always needs the reboot, with or without an AI accelerator, because it changes the Raspberry Pi's boot settings for the camera and any accelerator it found. The services start after the reboot. After it, open http://<hostname>.local/, claim the device with the setup code, and continue with First-time setup. A device that isn't on a network you can reach runs its own hotspot. Join it with the password from the card, and your phone's sign-in window opens the setup page; see Wi-Fi and the hotspot.

The installer's flags, such as a different install folder or time zone, are listed in Installer options.

docs.title: Install from another computer
docs.text:
The same script can install or update one or more devices over SSH from a Linux or Mac computer. Each device needs Raspberry Pi OS, a network connection, and an address you can reach.

git clone https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor
bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -H <address>[,<address>] -l <username> -k -K
Flag Meaning -H The devices' hostnames or IP addresses, separated by commas -l The username you set when imaging the cards. It must be the same on every device. -k Ask for the SSH password -K Ask for the password for administrator rights. Raspberry Pi OS requires it.

Remote devices reboot by themselves when the install needs it. The installer prints a setup code for each device, labeled with the device's address. A remote run doesn't ask for a Wi-Fi country. It keeps the device's, or sets US when the device has none; add -w <code> to set another, as in Installer options. The hotspot's password isn't printed, because it would end up in the installer's log. Run sudo tm-control card on each device to read it.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
1. Choose a site and mount the device.
  2. First-time setup: claim the device, turn on detection, adjust the zones, and record the location.

docs.title: description: Add the Enviro+ air quality sensor to a Traffic Monitor: hardware, the sensor software, and the settings that connect it.
Air quality sensor
docs.text:
The optional air quality sensor measures gases, particulate matter, temperature, pressure, humidity, and light. Readings go into the device's database every five minutes and appear on the legacy dashboard.

We make no warranty on the accuracy of the sensor or its data. If you have an environmental science background, we'd welcome your help.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: The Pimoroni Enviro+ board with the Plantower PMS5003 particulate matter sensor, connected to the Raspberry Pi's GPIO header with a ribbon cable. The assembly steps show where the sensor sits in the enclosure. Pimoroni's getting started guide covers the board itself.

docs.title: Sensor software
docs.text:
The sensor is read by greendormer/enviroplus-monitor, a Python service that runs on the Raspberry Pi and publishes readings to the device's MQTT broker. Install it following that repository's instructions, then set these keys in its config.json (key reference):

Key Value Why enable_send_data_to_homemanager true Publish readings over MQTT mqtt_broker_name "localhost" The Traffic Monitor's broker, on port 1883 mqtt_username, mqtt_password The broker's login Needed once the broker has a login. See Connect from other devices. indoor_outdoor_function "Outdoor" Use the outdoor topic outdoor_mqtt_topic "aq/sensorname01/readings" The topic must start with aq/, and the middle part is the sensor's name in the Traffic Monitor's settings enable_display false The board's screen is inside the enclosure long_update_delay 300 Seconds between readings

Set the location keys for your site as well. The software uses them to calibrate the pressure and gas readings for altitude, and to work out sunrise and sunset:

{
    "altitude": 49,
    "city_name": "Portland",
    "time_zone": "America/Los_Angeles",
    "custom_locations": [
        "Portland, United States of America, America/Los_Angeles, 45.52, -122.681944"
    ]
}

docs.title: Turn the sensor on in the Traffic Monitor
docs.text:
In /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml, under sensors: airquality_monitors:, set the sensor's entry to enabled: true. The entry's name must match the middle part of the MQTT topic:

sensors:
    airquality_monitors:
        sensorname01:
            enabled: true

The change takes effect when you save the file. Readings from a sensor that isn't enabled are dropped.

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
• The first readings arrive after the sensor's stabilization period, five minutes by default (startup_stabilisation_time in config.json).
  • The gas readings are reported as uncalibrated for the first 100 minutes, while the gas sensor warms up.
  • Readings show in the Air Quality section of the legacy dashboard at http://<device>/ui/, and are stored in the airquality table. Air quality describes the payload and the columns.
  • The Raspberry Pi and the AI accelerator give off heat. The enclosure separates the sensor from them, but temperature and humidity may still read high.

docs.title: Plate Recognizer
docs.text:
Plate Recognizer is an optional add-on built on a commercial product from Plate Recognizer, a company the Traffic Monitor project isn't affiliated with. It's off unless you install it. The add-on runs the company's on-device license plate reader in a container next to Frigate. For each car event from a camera you choose that passed through zone_radar, it reads the plate from Frigate's snapshot and stores the plate number, region, and vehicle make, model, and color.

Frigate has its own license plate recognition, which the Traffic Monitor doesn't turn on.

Danger

Plates identify people. With this add-on on, the database is no longer de-identified: the plate_recognizer table holds plate numbers. Keep the database on the device, don't share it, and make sure your use complies with local law. See Data and privacy.

You need a Plate Recognizer account with an on-premise (SDK) license, which gives you an API token and a license key.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
1. Run the installer with the add-on turned on:

    bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -C plate_recognizer

  2. Enter your API token and license key on the control app's Device page, under Tokens and keys. Saving each one restarts the add-on.

  3. Add the add-on's address to /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml, and turn the add-on on for each camera whose events should be read:

    sensors:
    cameras:
        picam_h265:
            enabled: true
            plate_recognizer: true

addons:
    plate_recognizer:
        url: http://plate-recognizer:8080

    Node-RED picks up config.yml as soon as you save it, so it needs no restart.

  4. Optionally, set WORKERS in /opt/traffic-monitor/plate-recognizer/plate-recognizer.env to the number of plates to read in parallel. 2 suits a Raspberry Pi 5. After you change it, restart the add-on with sudo systemctl restart plate-recognizer.service.

Upgrading a device that already reads plates

The installer moves a token and license key you typed into the add-on's env file, and a token in config.yml, to the device's secrets. Plate reads carry on without you entering them again. The Device page shows them as set.

Frigate's snapshots must stay on, which they are by default; the reader works from them.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
Each read goes into the plate_recognizer table, keyed by the event it belongs to.

Column Type Meaning event_id TEXT, primary key The id of the event filename TEXT The snapshot that was read timestamp TEXT The event's frame_time, when Frigate took the best frame of the car camera_id TEXT Always picam_h264, whichever camera the event came from processing_time REAL Milliseconds the read took plate_type TEXT Plate category, if the reader reports one plate_score REAL Confidence that a plate was found, 0 to 1 plate_xmin, plate_ymin, plate_xmax, plate_ymax INTEGER The plate's box in the snapshot, in pixels plate_value TEXT The plate number plate_value_score REAL Confidence in the plate number, 0 to 1 plate_region_value TEXT The issuing region, such as us-or. The reader looks only for us, us-or, and us-wa plates. plate_region_score REAL Confidence in the region, 0 to 1 vehicle_type TEXT Vehicle category, such as Sedan vehicle_score REAL Confidence in the vehicle, 0 to 1 vehicle_xmin, vehicle_ymin, vehicle_xmax, vehicle_ymax INTEGER The vehicle's box in the snapshot, in pixels vehicle_make, vehicle_model TEXT Make and model vehicle_make_model_score REAL Confidence in make and model, 0 to 1 vehicle_orientation TEXT Front, Rear, or similar vehicle_orientation_score REAL Confidence in the orientation, 0 to 1 vehicle_color TEXT Color vehicle_color_score REAL Confidence in the color, 0 to 1 json_payload TEXT The reader's full JSON response

docs.title: Build your own
docs.text:
A Traffic Monitor is a Raspberry Pi 5, a camera, an optional radar and AI accelerator, and a weather-resistant enclosure. Building one takes an afternoon.

  1. Hardware: the parts list, with the options that have been tested.
  2. Assembly: fitting the parts into the 3D-printed enclosure.
  3. Install the software: image the microSD card and run the installer.
  4. Update the software: when a new release comes out.

Then continue with Choose a site and mount and First-time setup.

docs.text:
Attach the ribbon cable to the Raspberry Pi's GPIO pins with the notch on top.

Attach the ribbon cable with the notch toward the outside of the Raspberry Pi
  • Pre-fold the cable so it lies flat when the case is closed.
  • The connector is tight on the pins and close to the cooler's heatsink. Work it down a few millimeters at a time, side to side, until it's fully seated.

docs.title: description: The parts for a Traffic Monitor: Raspberry Pi 5, camera, AI accelerator, radar, enclosure, power, and the optional air quality sensor.
Hardware
docs.text:
The core parts are the Raspberry Pi 5, a microSD card, a camera, and an AI accelerator. A radar adds accurate speeds, and an air quality sensor adds environmental readings. You can swap parts, but the docs and the default settings assume the parts below.

What each combination gives you:

  1. Camera and AI accelerator: object detection and counts. The lowest cost.
  2. Add a radar for speeds and the direction of travel. Without a radar, events have no speed or direction.
  3. Add an air quality sensor for gases, particulate matter, temperature, pressure, humidity, and light.
  4. Add cameras to watch more directions with the same accelerator. The software supports several cameras and up to four radars, paired in any pattern. See Cameras.

docs.title: Parts list
docs.text:
We are not affiliated with the stores or companies linked here. These are parts contributors have used or tested; if you've tested others, post in the discussions.

  • Computer: Raspberry Pi 5, 4 GB or 8 GB
    • Power: the official 27 W USB-C power supply
    • Cooling: the Raspberry Pi active cooler
  • Storage: a microSD card of 32 GB or more, such as the Raspberry Pi SD card or the SanDisk Extreme Pro
  • Camera: Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3, wide angle, plus a Raspberry Pi 5 camera cable
  • AI accelerator: see AI accelerator
  • Radar (recommended): OmniPreSense OPS243-A
  • Enclosure: see Enclosure
  • Air quality sensor (optional): Enviro+ with the PMS5003 particulate matter sensor and a male-to-female GPIO ribbon cable
  • Screws: assorted M3 for the boards and enclosure, M2.5×10 mm for the Raspberry Pi

docs.title: Computer
docs.text:
The Raspberry Pi 5 with 4 GB of memory runs the standard setup. Choose 8 GB if you plan to add sensors or other applications. Add the active cooler; it's inexpensive and prevents throttling on hot days.

Warning

The Raspberry Pi 4 and earlier can't supply enough power over USB for the accelerator and the radar together, which causes resets and dropped readings. Some people have run object detection alone on older models.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: A good microSD card of 32 GB or more holds the system and the database. Both the Raspberry Pi SD card and the SanDisk Extreme Pro have been tested. An NVMe (M.2) drive is faster and more durable, and some M.2 HATs hold both a drive and a Coral accelerator.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
The Raspberry Pi 5 needs a 27 W supply (5 V at 5 A). A weaker supply, such as an older Raspberry Pi adapter, causes resets and throttling. The device itself draws 6 to 14 W while detecting, and every part is powered from the Raspberry Pi.

  • Mains: the official 27 W USB-C power supply.
  • Power over Ethernet: a PoE HAT such as the Waveshare PoE HAT (F) or Waveshare PoE M.2 HAT+, with a PoE+ source such as the Raspberry Pi PoE+ injector.
  • Battery for about a day: a portable power station such as a Jackery Explorer 300, with the official power supply plugged into it. A 300 Wh station lasts about a day.
Longer off-grid use: custom battery and solar

Battery. Use a 12 V or 24 V LiFePO₄ battery and a buck converter that steps it down to 5 V at 5 A. Size the battery from the device's draw of about 13 W: a 12 V, 10 Ah battery (120 Wh) lasts about 9 hours, and 24 hours needs 13 × 24 = 312 Wh, a 12 V battery of about 30 Ah.

Solar. Add a photovoltaic panel and a charge controller to the battery setup. Size the panel for the worst month:

  1. Look up your daily solar potential. Portland, Oregon, gets about 7.15 kWh/day in summer and 1.42 kWh/day in winter per kW of panel.
  2. Multiply by the panel size. A 100 W panel in a Portland winter produces about 1.42 × 0.1 = 142 Wh per day.
  3. Allow for the controller. A PWM controller passes about 80%, so 142 × 0.8 = 113 Wh per day.
  4. Compare with the 312 Wh the device uses per day. A 100 W panel isn't enough; a Portland winter needs about 300 W of panel.

Real output depends on panel angle, cloud, shade from trees, and snow. This setup is a prototype, not a tested product.

docs.title: Cameras
docs.text:
The Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 in its wide-angle version is the tested camera. It needs the Raspberry Pi 5 camera cable, sold separately. The Raspberry Pi Global Shutter camera has been tested too, for faster motion or a custom lens, with the same cable. It needs camera stream settings that match its sensor, because the defaults are for Camera Module 3. They're in /var/lib/go2rtc/go2rtc.yaml, which every update replaces, so redo them after updating.

The Raspberry Pi 5 has two camera connectors, so it can take two Raspberry Pi cameras. Network cameras also work; see Frigate's camera recommendations. Choose one that streams H.265 (HEVC), which the Raspberry Pi 5 decodes in hardware. H.264 works with software decoding but costs CPU, so keep to one or two such cameras.

docs.title: AI accelerator
docs.text:
An AI accelerator runs the object detection model at over 100 frames per second with a few milliseconds per inference, enough for several cameras. Without one, Frigate detects on the CPU, which is slower and misses more objects on a busy road, so an accelerator is recommended for any deployment with a camera.

  1. Recommended: Raspberry Pi AI HAT+ with the Hailo-8 or Hailo-8L.
  2. Older: Coral USB Accelerator. It has become expensive and hard to find.
  3. Older: Coral M.2 Accelerator B+M key (not the A+E key) on the Raspberry Pi M.2 HAT+.

Frigate's supported detectors lists other options. The installer detects the Coral and Hailo accelerators and configures Frigate for whichever it finds.

docs.title: Radar
docs.text: The OmniPreSense OPS243-A Doppler radar measures speed and direction up to about 100 m away and is certified with the same tests as law-enforcement speed radars. It connects over USB.

docs.title: Air quality sensor
docs.text: The Enviro+ board with the PMS5003 particulate matter sensor measures gases, particulates, temperature, pressure, humidity, and light. It plugs into the Raspberry Pi's GPIO header through a male-to-female ribbon cable, which reaches the sensor's place in the enclosure. Air quality sensor covers the software.

docs.title: Enclosure
docs.text:
• Print it. The 3D-printable enclosure is open source at greendormer/tm-enclosure-3d, with a parts list.

  • Adapt a junction box. A waterproof electrical box of about 9 × 7 × 4 inches, such as the TICONN IP67 ABS enclosure, holds the parts, the camera, and the radar with some modification.

docs.title: Update the software
docs.text: An update reruns the installer from a newer copy of the repository. Your data and your settings stay; the containers are rebuilt.

docs.title: Before you update
docs.text:
• Read the release notes. A release that needs a fresh image says so.
  • Download a copy of the database from the Data export page.
  • Make sure the device has an internet connection. The update downloads packages and rebuilds the container images. Rebuilding Frigate's image compiles ffmpeg on the device, which can take about 20 minutes.

docs.title: Update
docs.text:
Connect to the device over SSH, then update the clone you installed from and rerun the whole installer:

cd traffic-monitor
git pull
bash script/tmsetup.sh

Run the whole installer rather than a single tag, because one version's changes can span several components.

Restart when the installer asks. When the services come back, the Node-RED service applies any database schema changes before it opens the database. Schema versions describes the copy it saves first.

Every app asks for the device's login, and the Node-RED editor has no login of its own: it opens for the device's administrator. If the device has no administrator account yet, every page opens the setup page instead. Claim the device with the setup code from the end of the installer's output; until the device is claimed, sudo cat /etc/traffic-monitor/setup-code also shows it. Control app and login walks through setup and adding accounts.

The installer printed tm-control migrate: WARNING or ERROR

The installer brings Frigate's configuration up to date, moves the ThingsBoard and Plate Recognizer tokens out of config.yml and the add-on's env file and a Frigate+ key out of frigate.env, and warns about what it can't change safely. An ERROR line means the installer stopped; the last item below covers the two causes. Each warning names the camera, stream, setting, or file. To find the warnings later:

grep -E 'tm-control migrate: (WARNING|ERROR)' ~/tmsetup-*.log

A camera input or stream without a login. A camera's input path in Frigate's configuration reads a stream on port 8554 without a login. If that path points at this device, for example by its IP address, add {FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_USER}:{FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_PASSWORD}@ before the host in Frigate's configuration editor. The higher-resolution stream section shows a complete path. If it points at another device, leave it as it is.

An auth, proxy, or tls setting. The installer adds the settings that turn off Frigate's own login and let Frigate trust the user and role that the device's login passes on. It leaves a section that's already there as it is, and warns when a setting in it would get in the way:

  • auth.enabled or tls.enabled is true or missing: Frigate asks for its own login as well as the device's, or serves its port over TLS, which the device doesn't use.
  • A proxy setting doesn't match, followed by auth was not added when the file had no auth section: Frigate could trust user and role headers the device doesn't set, so the installer leaves Frigate's own login on.

Change each named setting to match the default Frigate config, in /opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/config/config.yml over SSH. Then run bash script/tmsetup.sh -t frigate, which adds what's still missing, and restart Frigate with sudo systemctl restart frigate.service.

A token or key that wasn't moved. The installer moves a ThingsBoard token, a Plate Recognizer token, and a license key that it finds in config.yml or in plate-recognizer.env, and a Frigate+ key typed into frigate.env, to the device's secrets, and deletes the keys from config.yml. It leaves a value that isn't text, or that has a character a token can't have, such as a space, and warns about it. A Frigate+ key moves only in the format Frigate+ shows it in, on its own or between double quotes; for a key it leaves, the installer writes the device's own key, or none, into frigate.env. It also warns when a value differs from the one the device already holds. The device keeps the value it holds, and config.yml and the env files are backed up with a timestamp, so the other value stays in the backup. That backup's name ends in .migrate.bak, and it stays until you delete it. Enter the token on the control app's Device page, or the Frigate+ key on its Detection page, and delete a key the installer left in config.yml.

A file that is a symbolic link, or a YAML error (ERROR). The installer refuses to change a config.yml or env file that is a symbolic link, and stops. Replace the link with the file itself, then run the installer again. A YAML error in Node-RED's config.yml also stops the installer, as one in Frigate's does. Fix the error in /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml, then run the installer again.

A Frigate configuration from a backup may lack the camera stream login and the proxy settings. After you restore one, run bash script/tmsetup.sh -t frigate to add them.

Port 1883 accepts MQTT connections only from the device itself unless the broker has a login. If a display board, Home Assistant, or another device on your network reads MQTT from this device, give the broker a login and give it to that device; see Connect from other devices.

Open http://<device>/, log in, and check the Monitoring dashboard for new counts. After an update from a version without the Location page, that first visit to the control app also sets up the device's places; see Places after an update.

To update several devices from your computer, use the remote form of the installer described in Install the software.

docs.title: Places after an update
docs.text:
An update from a version without the control app's Location page brings the location settings up to date:

  • The installer adds database_precision: '2' to config.yml, so the database stores the location rounded to about 1 km. It removes any lat and lon under a camera or radar, because the location belongs to the whole device, and its output names each sensor.
  • When Node-RED first starts, it saves a copy of the database, gives each location in the stored rows a place id, and rounds the stored coordinates to two decimal places, once. The copy keeps the exact rows until the next update that changes the database replaces it; see Schema versions.

Then open the control app and log in, as any user. The first time its home page, Status page, or Location page opens after Node-RED has started, the control app sets up the device's places:

  • Each location in the saved copy becomes a used place, marked Imported from your previous settings.
  • The place at the location in config.yml becomes the place in use, and the control app writes its id into config.yml, so the deployments running now carry on. If no imported place is at that location, for example because it changed while the device was off, the control app makes a new place from config.yml, and new deployments start.
  • A device with no location in config.yml gets a new place in use with no location. Its past places are imported all the same.

Open the control app before the next update

The control app reads the past places from the saved copy, and the next update that changes the database replaces it. Open the control app before then, and keep the copy until the Location page lists the places. If Node-RED hasn't answered yet, the Status page's Location check says the places haven't been set up, and the control app tries again each time a page that shows the checks opens.

If there's no copy, or the control app can't read it, the control app skips the import and makes only the place in use, from config.yml. The past places' records stay in the database, grouped by place id, but the Location page doesn't list those places.

A device whose sensors had their own coordinates

The update gives each sensor's own location a place of its own. Once the control app writes the place in use into config.yml, each sensor whose location differed from the device's starts a new deployment there. Its earlier records stay with their own place, which the Location page lists as used.

docs.title: What an update changes
docs.text:
An update replaces the container images, service units, Node-RED flows, and the reverse proxy configuration. It keeps your settings files, the database, Frigate's recordings, and the device's accounts. With -f, it also replaces the settings files with fresh copies from the templates and keeps each old file beside the new one with a timestamp. What -f replaces lists the files.

Use -f when a release changes the settings files and you want the new template. Afterwards, turn Frigate's detection back on and redo your settings from the timestamped copies: the sensors section of config.yml, and zones in Frigate. First-time setup walks through each. You don't need to copy back survey_id, lat, lon, database_precision, or the bearings: the next time the control app is opened, it puts back the place in use, its location, the precision you chose, and the way each sensor faces there; see Edit the location by hand.

Node-RED flow changes made in the editor on the device are replaced on every update. Commit them to the repository instead; see Dev environment.

docs.title: Update one component
docs.text:
Each installer tag reruns one component, plus anything that has to change with it; see Tags. For example, after plugging in a radar:

bash script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm

Installer options lists the tags and flags.

docs.title: description: The variables in node-red-tm.env and frigate.env: radar serial ports, database path, MQTT broker, the Frigate+ key, and the values the installer fills in.
Env file settings
docs.text: Two env files hold the environment that the Node-RED and Frigate containers start with. The installer writes each from its template on the first install and leaves it alone afterwards, unless you run the installer with -f. Most devices never need either edited.

docs.title: node-red-tm.env
docs.text:
/opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/node-red-tm.env is written from this template.

After editing it, restart the service:

sudo systemctl restart node-red-tm.service

After changing the MQTT broker login

A restart or reboot isn't enough after you change TM_MQTT_BROKER_USERNAME or TM_MQTT_BROKER_PASSWORD. Run the installer instead, so Frigate gets the same login and port 1883 opens or closes to match:

bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm

Otherwise the broker refuses Frigate's connection, and no events are recorded.

Variable Default Meaning TM_VERSION the installed release The Traffic Monitor version, shown on the dashboards and sent with telemetry. The installer sets it; don't edit it. TM_RPI_SN the Raspberry Pi's serial number Identifies the device in ThingsBoard, and fills deviceName in deployment records. Set by the installer. TM_HOSTNAME the device's hostname at install Prefix for the file names of data exports. Set by the installer. NODE_RED_CREDENTIAL_SECRET myNodeRED1234 Encrypts the credentials saved in the Node-RED editor. Leave it as it is: every installer run copies in the repository's credentials file, which is encrypted with this default, so a changed value leaves Node-RED unable to read it. TM_NR_TOKEN_KEY generated on the device Lets the Node-RED editor check that the device's login let you in. The installer sets it on every run; leave it. Without it, the editor refuses everyone. TM_THINGSBOARD_ACCESS_TOKEN the token you set, or empty The device's access token for the ThingsBoard upload. The installer fills it from the device's secrets on every run; change it on the Device page, not here. Empty keeps the upload off. TM_PLATE_RECOGNIZER_TOKEN the token you set, or empty The API token for the Plate Recognizer add-on. Filled and changed the same way. Empty keeps plate reads off. TM_INTERNAL_TOKEN generated on the device Lets the control app read Node-RED's state for the Status page. The installer sets it on every run; leave it. Without it, the Status page can't read Node-RED's state. TM_DATABASE_PATH_TMDB /db/tmdb.sqlite The database, as seen inside the container. On the device it's /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/db/tmdb.sqlite. Leave it; schema migrations and downloads expect this path. TM_MQTT_BROKER_HOST localhost The MQTT broker that Node-RED hosts. Frigate and the air quality sensor publish to it. See MQTT and ThingsBoard. TM_MQTT_BROKER_PORT 1883 The broker's port. TM_MQTT_BROKER_USERNAME empty The broker's login username. When it and the password are both set, the broker requires the login from every client, and port 1883 opens to the network. Letters, digits, ., _, and - only, with no quotes and no comment after the value. See Connect from other devices. TM_MQTT_BROKER_PASSWORD empty The broker's login password, with the same rules as the username. TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00 to TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_03 /dev/ttyACM0 to /dev/ttyACM3 The serial port of each radar. The variable's name is the radar's name in config.yml. The installer passes only the ports that exist at install time into the container, so after plugging in a radar rerun bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm.

docs.title: frigate.env
docs.text:
/opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/frigate.env is written from this template. After editing it, restart Frigate with sudo systemctl restart frigate.service.

Variable Default Meaning FRIGATE_RTSP_PASSWORD password A password for cameras of your own: Frigate fills in {FRIGATE_RTSP_PASSWORD} in a camera's input path. The Traffic Monitor's own camera doesn't use it. The installer leaves it as you set it, unless you run it with -f. PLUS_API_KEY the key you set, or empty The Frigate+ API key. The installer fills it from the device's secrets on every run; change it on the Detection page, not here. Empty means no key: Frigate can't submit snapshots or download a Frigate+ model.

The other lines are the installer's. Leave them as they are:

  • FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_USER and FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_PASSWORD: the login Frigate reads the device's camera stream with.
  • FRIGATE_PROXY_AUTH_SECRET: lets Frigate trust who the device's login says you are.
  • FRIGATE_MQTT_USER and FRIGATE_MQTT_PASSWORD: Frigate's login to the MQTT broker, which follows the broker login in node-red-tm.env.
  • FRIGATE_HOME_DIR, FRIGATE_VERSION, and FRIGATE_BASE_PATH: where Frigate's files are, its version, and the /frigate/ path it's served at.

docs.title: Tune object detection
docs.text:
Frigate does the object detection. How well it works depends on the mounting height and angle, the camera, and the weather, so expect to adjust it for each site. The Traffic Monitor is not affiliated with the Frigate project.

The Traffic Monitor's default Frigate config is tuned for roadways seen from an oblique angle, with a side view of objects as they pass. Everything in it can be changed in Frigate's own UI, at Settings > Configuration editor, when you're logged in to the device as the administrator. Frigate's configuration reference explains every setting.

Frigate's own login is off. The device's login passes your username and role on to Frigate: the administrator gets Frigate's admin role, and viewers its viewer role, which can watch and review but not change settings. Frigate's Logout logs you out of the device. Keep auth: enabled: false and the proxy: section as they are; with Frigate's login on, Frigate asks for a second login of its own, separate from the device's accounts.

docs.title: See what Frigate sees
docs.text:
Go to Settings > Debug to watch detections live with their scores, and the motion regions Frigate is checking. Explore lists past detections with their snapshots, which is the quickest way to find missed bikes or a tree that's being called a person.

The debug view shows how detection is performing

docs.title: Object filters
docs.text:
Frigate tracks bicycle, person, car, bus, motorcycle, and dog by default. Each object type has two scores in the objects: filters: section of the config:

  • min_score is the score needed to start tracking an object.
  • threshold is the average score an object needs, over the time it's tracked, to count as a real detection.

The defaults set bicycle low, so most kinds of bike are detected, and motorcycle high, so a large e-bike isn't called a motorcycle. If you see false positives for a type, raise its threshold; if you miss objects, lower it. Frigate's object filters page describes these and the size and shape filters.

docs.title: Masks
docs.text:
Go to Settings > Camera configuration > Masks / Zones.

  • A motion mask stops motion in an area, such as swaying branches or a timestamp overlay, from triggering detection.
  • An object mask ignores detections of one object type in an area, such as a parked car that's detected every time the light changes.

Warning

Use masks sparingly. Over-masking makes objects harder to track. A motion mask isn't the tool for cutting false positives; adjust the object filters first.

Frigate's masks page has the details.

docs.title: Higher-resolution stream
docs.text:
The Pi camera is set up to produce two streams. Frigate uses picam_h265_detect at 1536×864 by default, which gives the best balance of detail and load. A second stream, picam_h265_detect_hr, runs at 2304×1296 for cases where objects are small in the frame.

To switch, change two things in the configuration editor under cameras: picam_h265:: the input path to rtsp://{FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_USER}:{FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_PASSWORD}@host.containers.internal:8554/picam_h265_detect_hr, and detect: width: 2304 with height: 1296. Frigate fills in the {…} values from frigate.env. Then redraw the zones for the new frame size. The higher resolution costs CPU and may lower the frame rate on a busy road.

docs.title: Recordings and snapshots
docs.text:
By default, Frigate keeps a cropped snapshot of each detection and a recording of each alert and detection for about an hour, so you can check what was detected. The record: and snapshots: sections control this: set enabled: false to keep nothing, or raise retain: days to keep more. Data and privacy describes what the device stores.

Frigate can also publish a cropped snapshot of each detected object on the device's MQTT broker. The Traffic Monitor doesn't use these snapshots, so new installs turn them off with mqtt: enabled: false under cameras: picam_h265:. On an older install, add those lines in the configuration editor. Frigate keeps publishing the events the Traffic Monitor counts.

cameras:
  picam_h265:
    mqtt:
      enabled: false

docs.title: Better models
docs.text: Frigate+ is a paid service from the Frigate project, separate from the Traffic Monitor. You submit snapshots from your device, label them on the Frigate+ website, and Frigate+ trains a model on them, which can raise accuracy for a difficult site. Its documentation covers the account, labeling, and training.

docs.title: Enter the key
docs.text: Frigate+ gives your account an API key. Enter it on the control app's Detection page, under Frigate+. The page checks the key's format, so a mis-pasted key is caught there. Saving or removing the key restarts Frigate, which takes about a minute. Traffic isn't counted until it's back.

docs.title: Submit snapshots
docs.text:
The key is all Frigate needs to submit snapshots. Open Explore in Frigate, select a detection, and submit its snapshot to Frigate+. The default config keeps snapshots on, but only for about an hour (see Recordings and snapshots), so submit them soon or keep them longer.

A snapshot you submit leaves the device: Frigate sends it to Frigate+, and it can show people.

docs.title: Use a model
docs.text:
A model trained by Frigate+ has to be built for the device's detector:

Device Detector type to choose in Frigate+ Coral accelerator edgetpu Hailo accelerator hailo8l No accelerator cpu

Choose the yolov9 model type; mobiledet is the older one. The Status page tells you which detector the device has, in its Hardware group.

To use a model on a device that's online, either:

  • pick it in Frigate's Settings > System > Detectors and model, or

  • in Settings > Configuration editor, replace the whole model: section with only the model's path, then choose Save & Restart:

    model:
  path: plus://<model id>

    Remove every other key under model:; Frigate+ supplies them.

Frigate checks a model before it saves the change: if the model isn't on the device yet, it fetches it with your key, and if the key is missing or wrong, the model id is wrong, or the device is offline, it refuses the change, shows why, and changes nothing. A model it accepts is on the device as two files in /opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/config/model_cache/, named after the model id: <model id> and <model id>.json. Frigate loads it when it restarts.

docs.title: A device without internet
docs.text:
Frigate downloads a model only when one of its two files is missing, so a device that's offline can use a Frigate+ model too:

  1. On another computer, download the model from Frigate+. You get two files: <model id> and <model id>.json.
  2. On the control app's Detection page, choose Upload a model and pick both files. You can also upload a package from whoever trained the model, or the two files from another device, which you can download from its Detection page.
  3. Choose Use on the model. Frigate reads the two files when it checks the config, without contacting Frigate+, and the device restarts Frigate. If either file is missing, Frigate refuses the change, because it would have to download the model.

The key is then needed only to submit snapshots, which takes internet as well.

docs.title: A model of your own
docs.text:
You can also run a model that doesn't come from Frigate+. On the Detection page, upload the model's file with its .json, or upload the file alone and fill in what Frigate needs to know about it; the page writes the .json. Choose Use, and the page writes the model's model: section for you: its path, input size, input layout, model type, and label map.

To do it by hand instead, copy the model's file into /opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/config/model_cache/ over SSH, and set path: /config/model_cache/<file> in the model: section. Unlike a plus:// model, it also needs the keys that describe it: width, height, input_tensor, input_pixel_format, input_dtype, model_type, and labelmap_path. Frigate's reference config lists their values. The model must suit the device's detector, as a Frigate+ model must.

docs.title: What the installer keeps
docs.text: Running the installer with -f replaces Frigate's config with a fresh copy, but keeps the model: section you chose, however you set it, as long as it isn't the installer's own model. Comments inside the section are lost. After you change the accelerator, a kept model may not suit the new one, and the Status page says so. What -f replaces and Add an accelerator later have the details.

docs.title: The Frigate+ check
docs.text:
The Status page's Configuration group has a Frigate+ check. It compares the key with the model: section of Frigate's config and says whether Frigate could use the model:

Status Meaning Passed Frigate+ isn't in use: no key and no Frigate+ model. Or Frigate runs the Frigate+ model the config names. Without a key, it runs from the files on the device, and you can't submit snapshots. Warning A key is set, but Frigate runs the installer's model, its own default model (on a device with no model: section), or one of your own. Snapshots can be submitted. Once Frigate+ has trained a model, set it as in Use a model. Problem Frigate can't use the Frigate+ model the config names. Either no key is set and the model's files aren't on the device, so Frigate can't download it (Set the key opens the Frigate+ API key section of the Detection page), or the model isn't built for the device's detector; where Frigate's log says why, the check quotes it. Also a problem: the model id has characters an id can't have, or Frigate isn't answering and its log has an error, which the check quotes. When Frigate+ gave Frigate no token for the key, as with a wrong key, the check says so, and Set the key opens the Frigate+ API key section of the Detection page. See If Frigate stops over a model. Couldn't run Frigate's config is missing or isn't valid YAML, or Frigate isn't answering and its log has no error to quote. Or Frigate is in safe mode for a reason other than the model, so whether it can use the model is unknown; the Apps group's Frigate check says why.

When Frigate can't use its config, for example because of a model built for another detector, it starts in safe mode: it answers and looks healthy, but has no cameras and counts nothing. The Apps group's Frigate check reports that as a problem, whatever the cause, and quotes Frigate's messages. Fix the config in Frigate's configuration editor, then choose Save & Restart.

docs.title: If Frigate stops over a model
docs.text:
Frigate refuses a model it can't fetch when you save, so it ends up with one only in ways that skip that check:

  • you edit Frigate's config.yml over SSH,
  • the installer keeps the model: section with -f after the key was removed, or
  • the key is removed or changed while the model's files aren't on the device yet.

Frigate then fails each time it starts, restarts every few seconds, and counts nothing. On the Status page, Frigate's row in the Services group says it restarted after failures, and the Frigate and Frigate+ checks quote the last error in Frigate's log.

To get Frigate running again, do one of these:

  1. On the Detection page, under Other models on this device, choose Use on The installer's model (on a device without a Coral, on Frigate's built-in model). While Frigate isn't answering, the device edits Frigate's config itself and restarts Frigate.
  2. Enter the right key on the Detection page, under Frigate+. Saving it restarts Frigate, which then fetches the model.
  3. Upload the model's two files on the Detection page, as in A device without internet, and choose Use.
  4. As a last resort, over SSH, open Frigate's config as root with sudo nano /opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/config/config.yml and replace its model: section with the installer's. Copy it from the default Frigate config, where its path names the .tflite file in model_cache, or from a backup beside the file, if an earlier run of the installer with -f left one. Only a device with a Coral has that section; on another device, delete the model: section. Then restart Frigate with sudo systemctl restart frigate.service.

Running the installer with -f doesn't help, because it keeps the model: section.

Info

A wrong key on its own never stops Frigate. When it starts, Frigate contacts Frigate+ only to download a model whose files are missing, so a model whose files are on the device keeps running whatever the key.

docs.title: config.yml settings
docs.text:
The Traffic Monitor's own settings live in /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml on the device. The installer writes it from this template on the first install and leaves it alone afterwards, unless you run the installer with -f.

The Traffic Monitor reads the file again whenever you save it, so changes take effect without a restart. If the file has a YAML error, it keeps the previous settings until the service restarts, and after a restart it has no settings at all until you fix the file.

Keep the three top-level sections (thingsboard, deployment, sensors) in the file. The file has no time settings: the installer's -z option sets the device's time zone, and you change it later on the Date and time page. A time section left from an older install is ignored. The Default column below shows the values the template writes. A setting that's missing from the file behaves differently in a few cases:

  • A camera or radar without enabled is off.
  • A radar without opt_api_commands_array gets no extra commands.
  • ThingsBoard without host stays off.
  • A camera whose camera_radar names a radar that isn't in the file records no events. On a device without a radar, remove camera_radar or keep the radar's entry with enabled: false.

docs.title: thingsboard
docs.text:
Uploads events, readings, and device telemetry to a ThingsBoard server. See MQTT and ThingsBoard.

Setting Type Default Meaning enabled true or false false Turn the upload on. host text tb.server.com (a placeholder) The server's hostname. If it starts with http:// or https://, that is used and protocol is ignored. Required when enabled. protocol http or https https How to reach the server. port number none Set it only if the server isn't on the standard port for the protocol.

The device's access token isn't in this file. Set it on the control app's Device page; it's kept with the device's other secrets.

docs.title: deployment
docs.text:
Where the device is. Every event and reading is stored with a deployment id that points at these values. The control app's Location page writes them when you claim the device, deploy it to a place, change the precision, or correct a value, so you rarely edit them here. All of them are optional.

Setting Type Default Meaning survey_id <8 lower-case hex digits>-si, such as 3f9a1c2e-si empty The place in use, with no coordinates in it. The Location page writes it. Each device makes its own ids, and two devices never need to share one. Upper case is folded to lower case; an id in any other form is ignored and logged as an error. database_precision none, 1, or 2 '2' How many decimal places of lat and lon the database keeps: none stores no coordinates, 1 about 10 km, 2 about 1 km. A number without quotes works too. lat decimal degrees, such as 45.52252 empty Latitude of the place in use, optional, with five decimal places at most. The database stores it rounded to database_precision; this file and the control app keep the exact value. lon decimal degrees, such as -122.69120 empty Longitude, optional, with the same rules as lat. Set both or neither: a row with only one gets neither. bearing n, s, e, w, ne, nw, se, or sw empty The compass direction the camera and radar face. Optional; a value that isn't one of these, including one with spaces around it, is logged as an error.

A change of survey_id, or of a sensor's bearing, closes that sensor's current deployment and starts a new one. A change of lat or lon doesn't. While survey_id is empty, current deployments stay as they are, and a bearing change waits until you set one. When you first set survey_id, a current deployment with no survey id and the same bearing takes it over and keeps its deployment id.

Lowering database_precision rewrites the current deployments in place. Raising it takes effect from the next new deployment, because coordinates already rounded can't be made finer. The Location page can also round the rows already stored; see Choose the precision.

A deployment: block under a camera or radar can hold bearing, for a device whose cameras face different ways. A lat or lon there isn't read, because the location belongs to the whole device. The installer removes it, and the Status page's Location check warns about it until then.

docs.title: Edit the location by hand
docs.text:
Use the Location page to move the device or fix a value. If you edit this section by hand instead, Node-RED applies the change as soon as you save the file, and the control app records it the next time it's opened, on its home page, Status page, or Location page:

  • survey_id set to a place the page lists is a move there. The file takes that place's location, replacing any lat or lon you changed in the same edit. Node-RED starts the new deployments as soon as you save, at the location the file held then, and the control app gives them the place's location when it records the move. If the place has no location, those deployments keep the one the file held.
  • survey_id set to an id the page doesn't list becomes a new place, in use, at this file's lat and lon.
  • Only lat or lon changed is a correction of the place in use, as Correct location would be: the place's stored rows take the new location.
  • survey_id emptied, as tmsetup.sh -f leaves it, is put back: the control app writes the place in use's id into the file again, and gives each sensor with an empty bearing the way it faces at that place. A bearing you set stays. database_precision goes back to the last value the control app saw while the file named a place, because after a reset the file holds the template's '2'. A coarser value you typed into the reset file stays. To choose a finer one, use the Location page, or edit the file once survey_id is back. If the place has a location, lat and lon get it back, whatever the file holds, because after a reset they come from the installer, not from you; correct a place's location on the Location page. If the place has none, a location in the file is a correction, as above. A typo stays as you typed it.
  • lat and lon both emptied, when the place in use has a location, are put back too, because a place's location can be corrected but not removed. To keep the location out of the database, choose No location stored as the precision.
  • A lat or lon that isn't a number in range, such as one with a typo, stays in the file as you typed it. New deployments store no location until you fix it, and the Status page's Location check names the key.

On a device upgraded from a release that recorded coordinates, the update leaves survey_id empty, and the control app fills it in the first time it's opened after Node-RED has started; see Places after an update.

docs.title: sensors.cameras
docs.text:
One entry per camera, named exactly as the camera is named in Frigate. The default camera is picam_h265. Events from a camera that isn't listed here, or is disabled, are ignored.

To rename a camera, rename it in Frigate's config and choose Save & Restart. Frigate uses a new camera name only after it restarts, so Save alone changes nothing yet. Then rename its entry here to match. Until both names agree, that camera's events aren't recorded, and the Status page's Cameras in config.yml check shows an error.

Setting Type Default Meaning enabled true or false true for picam_h265 Record this camera's events. Frigate keeps running either way. camera_radar a radar name from sensors.radars TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00 The radar that supplies speeds for this camera. One radar can serve several cameras. Leave it out on a device without a radar. plate_recognizer true or false false Send this camera's events to the Plate Recognizer add-on. deployment block inherited Per-camera bearing.

docs.title: sensors.radars
docs.text:
One entry per radar. A radar's name is the name of the variable that holds its serial port in node-red-tm.env, TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00 through TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_03.

Setting Type Default Meaning enabled true or false true for TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00 Read this radar. Set it to false on a device without a radar. opt_api_commands_array a JSON array in a string '["^/+0.00\n", "^/-0.00\n"]' Extra OPS243 API commands sent to the radar when the service starts and whenever you save this file, after the Traffic Monitor's own setup commands. The default sets the cosine correction to 0 degrees in both directions. deployment block inherited Per-radar bearing.

docs.title: sensors.airquality_monitors
docs.text:
One entry per air quality sensor, named as the middle part of the topic the sensor publishes to: aq/<name>/readings.

Setting Type Default Meaning enabled true or false false Record this sensor's readings. Readings from a sensor that isn't enabled are dropped. mqtt_topic_incoming text readings Present in the template but not used. The device subscribes to every topic under aq/.

docs.title: addons.plate_recognizer
docs.text:
Only needed with the Plate Recognizer add-on. The section isn't in the template; add it.

Setting Type Default Meaning url URL none The add-on's address inside the device, http://plate-recognizer:8080.

The API token and license key aren't in this file. Set them on the control app's Device page; plates aren't read until they're set.

docs.title: Air quality
docs.text: The optional air quality sensor publishes a reading over MQTT every five minutes. The Traffic Monitor stores each reading as a row in the airquality table.

docs.title: MQTT payload
docs.text:
The sensor software publishes to aq/<sensor>/readings, where <sensor> is the sensor's name in config.yml. Readings are dropped unless that sensor is enabled there.

{
    "gas_calibrated": false,
    "bar": [1009.44, "0"],
    "hum": [28.7, "2"],
    "pm025": 0,
    "pm10": 0,
    "pm01": 0,
    "dew": 2.1,
    "temp": 21,
    "temp_min": 20.9,
    "temp_max": 21.1,
    "gas_red": 4.2,
    "gas_oxi": 0.15,
    "gas_nh3": 0.69,
    "lux": 1.2,
    "proximity": 255,
    "lux_raw": 1.16185,
    "temp_raw": 28.68982029794099,
    "bar_raw": 1003.7122773175154,
    "hum_raw": 18.31337919009301,
    "gas_red_raw": 140805,
    "gas_oxi_raw": 103585,
    "gas_nh3_raw": 227871,
    "current_time": 1738698665.077546
}

bar and hum are pairs: the value, then a comfort-level code ("0" stable to "4" storm for pressure; "1" good, "2" dry, "3" wet for humidity). Only the value is stored. temp_min, temp_max, and the sensor software's Forecast object aren't stored. The sensor software's README explains how it compensates and calibrates the readings.
