docs.text: Reading Sensor Notes Gases MiCS-6814 Measures resistance for reducing, oxidizing, and ammonia gases. The sensor software converts resistance to ppm, compensating for temperature, humidity, and pressure, and recalibrates daily for drift. Treat the ppm values as relative; see the discussion in pimoroni/enviroplus-python #47 and #67. Temperature, pressure, humidity BME280 The Raspberry Pi and AI accelerator warm the enclosure, so the compensated values are the ones to use. Pressure updates every 20 minutes. Light and proximity LTR-559 Noise SPH0645 MEMS microphone Not stored in the database Particulate matter Plantower PMS5003

docs.title: Data and privacy
docs.text: The Traffic Monitor is a data collection tool. Everything it collects is processed and stored on the device, in open formats, so you own it and can share it.

docs.title: What the device stores
docs.text: Where What How long /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/db/tmdb.sqlite The database: events, radar readings, air quality readings, the device's deployment history, and operator comments Until you delete it /opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/storage/ Frigate's cropped snapshots of each detection, and recordings of alerts and detections About an hour, by default Your ThingsBoard server A copy of the data above, plus system metrics If you turn on the ThingsBoard upload

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
We believe in open data: anonymized data is a public good and the basis of useful research. The database is designed to be shareable. With the default settings it is de-identified: it records what passed (a label), when, how fast, and through which zones, and never an image or a plate number. Its location is rounded to about 1 km, which in a town shows the neighbourhood but not the address.

Images do exist on the device, briefly. Frigate keeps snapshots and short clips for about an hour so you can check what it detected. To keep none, turn off recordings and snapshots as described in Tune object detection. To keep them longer, raise the retention there, and treat the device as holding images of people.

By default, the device sends no images or video anywhere. Everything is processed on the device, and tmdb.sqlite holds only metadata. The live view and the recordings are behind the device's login, which decides who on your network can open the apps. It isn't a control on the images themselves: anyone with an account on the device can see them, and they're ordinary files on the device's card. Frigate can also publish a snapshot of each detected object on the device's MQTT broker. New installs turn those snapshots off, and they stay on the device unless you give the broker a login, which opens it to your network. Tune object detection shows the setting. A snapshot you choose to submit to Frigate+ does leave the device, and it can show people.

With the default settings, the database is de-identified: it holds no images, plate numbers, or exact location. The place the device was used at is stored as a survey id, which has no coordinates in it, and any coordinates are rounded to about 1 km by default and never stored more precisely (see deployment). Where homes are far apart, a square about 1 km across may hold only one or two of them, so the rounded location can point to the house even though it isn't exact. If the device is at a home, especially in a rural area, choose About 10 km or No location stored on the Location page before it starts recording. The exact location stays on the device, in config.yml and in the control app's list of places, and neither is part of the database.

The database stops being de-identified if you:

  • Install the Plate Recognizer add-on. Plate numbers go into the plate_recognizer table. Don't share a database from a device that has ever had the add-on on.
  • Turn on Frigate features that add identifying sub-labels or attributes to events, such as face recognition or license plate recognition.
  • Write identifying details into operator comments.
  • Keep the copy of the database that an upgrade leaves in db/backup/. It can hold the exact coordinates from before they were rounded (see deployment), so don't share it.

For an area the camera shouldn't see at all, such as a window or a yard, aim the camera so the area is out of frame. A motion mask only stops motion there from starting a detection; the area still shows in the live view and in recordings.

Other software on the device, such as Frigate and the air quality sensor's service, keeps its own working data under its own retention rules.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Tables for sensors the device doesn't have stay empty.

Table Contents Could identify a person? events One row per object the camera detected, with direction and speed. See Events. Only through Frigate sub-labels or attributes, if you turn those on radar_dov Detected object velocity readings from the radar No radar_timed_speed_counts Counts and average speeds the radar reports every 300 seconds No radar_raw_speed_magnitude Raw speed and magnitude readings, three per sample No radar_raw_speed_magnitude_single The strongest reading of each sample No radar_oc_payload Per-object summaries from the radar, including estimated length No airquality Air quality and weather readings. See Air quality. No deployment Where each sensor was, and when No, except where homes are far apart: the location is rounded to about 1 km (two decimal places) by default and never stored more precisely, which in a rural area can point to a single home (see Privacy) comments Notes typed on the Data export page Possibly, if the operator types names plate_recognizer Plate reads from the Plate Recognizer add-on Yes

The radar tables are described on their own page. The two tables below have no other page.

docs.title: deployment
docs.text:
A row for each combination of sensor, survey, and bearing the device has had, taken from the deployment settings in config.yml. A new row starts when the survey id or the sensor's bearing changes; moving the coordinates alone does not start one. Every other table's deployment_id column holds the id of one of these rows, so you can tell where a reading was taken after the device has moved. The database declares no foreign key; it's a plain text column.

Column Type Meaning id TEXT, primary key The deployment id entryStartDateTime REAL Unix time, in milliseconds, when this deployment began entryEndDateTime REAL Unix time, in milliseconds, when it ended; empty for the current one survey_id TEXT The place: one id for each place the device has been used at, such as 3f9a1c2e-si. It has no coordinates in it, so rows at the same place share it. Empty when no survey id was set. location_precision INTEGER The number of decimal places kept in lat and lon: 1 (about 10 km) or 2 (about 1 km). Empty when the row has no coordinates. lat REAL Latitude in decimal degrees, rounded to location_precision decimal places; empty when no location was given or the precision is none lon REAL Longitude in decimal degrees, rounded the same way bearing TEXT Compass direction the sensor faces: n, s, e, w, ne, nw, se, or sw. Empty when no bearing was set; closed rows written by earlier releases can hold null or undefined instead. sensorType TEXT cameras, radars, or airquality_monitors sensorName TEXT The sensor's name in config.yml deviceName TEXT The Raspberry Pi's serial number (TM_RPI_SN in node-red-tm.env). Rows written by earlier releases can hold undefined instead.

The database holds shareable data only, so the exact location is never written to it. A database upgraded from a release that stored exact coordinates holds rounded ones. When Node-RED first starts after the upgrade, the database migration copies the database to db/backup/tmdb-v<N>-<time>.sqlite in the node-red-tm directory, where N is the schema version the device was on before, and that copy holds the exact rows. A device upgrading from a release (0.7.1 or earlier) has tmdb-v0-…, and a device that already ran a development build with the first schema version has tmdb-v1-…. The copy is kept until the next schema change succeeds. You can delete it sooner, once the control app has read the past places from it; see Places after an update. The first upgrade from a release copies the whole database, so it needs free space of about 1.2 times the database's size. If the disk was too full for the copy, it was skipped and the exact coordinates are gone.

docs.title: comments
docs.text:
Free-text notes an operator adds on the Data export page, for example "threshold lowered to 0.4" or "road work on the north side", so that whoever analyzes the data later knows what changed and when.

Column Type Meaning id TEXT, primary key effectiveDateTime TIMESTAMP When the note starts to apply expirationDateTime TIMESTAMP When it stops applying; empty if open-ended entryDateTime TIMESTAMP When it was written comment TEXT The note commenter_name TEXT Who wrote it

docs.title: Schema versions
docs.text:
The tables are defined by numbered migrations in the repository's container/node-red-tm/schema/ folder, and schema.sql there shows the whole current schema. Each time the Node-RED service starts, it applies any migrations the database doesn't have yet and records the schema version in the database. Before it does, it saves a copy of the database in /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/db/backup/ and keeps only the most recent copy. It makes no copy of a new database, or when the disk has less free space than about 1.2 times the database's size. It also makes none when the only migration to apply is the first, which only adds missing tables. You can read the version with PRAGMA user_version;.

If a migration fails, it's rolled back, and Node-RED starts on the previous version, which may not be able to save new data. The control app's Status page then shows Database schema as a problem. To see why, run sudo journalctl -u node-red-tm | grep tmdb-migrate, or download the diagnostics on the Device page. See the FAQ entry.

docs.title: Getting the data
docs.text:
• Download the whole database, or a JSON export of events, radar readings, or air quality readings over a date range, from the Data export page.
  • Open the database with DB Browser for SQLite, or from code with any SQLite library, such as Python's built-in sqlite3.
  • Subscribe to today's counts over MQTT, or upload everything to ThingsBoard. See MQTT and ThingsBoard.
  • Review snapshots and clips in Frigate's Explore view at http://<device>/frigate/.

docs.title: description: The events table: one row per object the camera detected, with its label, times, zones, direction, and radar speed.
Events
docs.text: An event is one object that Frigate detected and tracked until it left the frame: a car, a person, a bicycle, and so on. When the camera has a radar, the Traffic Monitor adds the direction of travel and the speed, and it stores the result in the events table of the database.

docs.title: How an event is made
docs.text:
1. Frigate publishes a message on the device's MQTT topic frigate/events for each tracked object. When the object leaves the frame, the message has type: "end" and holds everything Frigate knows about it.
  2. The Traffic Monitor keeps the end message if the camera is enabled in config.yml and the object moved.
  3. If the object entered any zone and the camera has an enabled radar, it works out the direction and the speed, as described below, and adds radar to provenance when a speed was found.
  4. It writes the row, publishes today's counts on tm/events, and uploads the event to ThingsBoard if that is on. See MQTT and ThingsBoard.

First-time setup describes the four zones.

docs.title: Direction and speed
docs.text:
The zones give a direction when the object entered both zone_near and zone_far: zone_near then zone_far is outbound, and the reverse is inbound. The radar's readings come from the time the object was in view, with a two-second margin on each side. The radar reports a direction with each reading, and the speed is the median of the readings in the chosen direction.

Zones Radar readings direction_calc speed_calc A direction In that direction, or in both directions The zones' direction The median in that direction A direction Only in the other direction Empty Empty No direction In one direction only The radar's direction The median in that direction No direction In both directions Empty Empty A direction None The zones' direction Empty No direction None Empty Empty

An object that entered no zone, and every object on a camera without an enabled radar, has no direction and no speed.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
Values that come straight from Frigate's message are marked Frigate. Frigate's MQTT page documents them in full.

Column Type Meaning Values id TEXT, primary key Frigate's event id Unix time in seconds, a hyphen, and six random characters, such as 1721144705.617111-fg3luy camera TEXT Frigate. The camera's name As named in Frigate, picam_h265 by default label TEXT Frigate. The object type One of Frigate's object labels sub_label TEXT Frigate. A label added by another process, such as a recognized face Usually empty top_score REAL Frigate. The highest detection score while the object was tracked 0 to 1 frame_time REAL Frigate. When the best frame of the object was taken Unix time in seconds start_time REAL Frigate. When the object was first seen Unix time in seconds end_time REAL Frigate. When the object was last seen Unix time in seconds entered_zones TEXT Frigate. The zones the object entered, in order A JSON array of zone names, such as ["zone_capture", "zone_near", "zone_radar", "zone_far"] score REAL Frigate. The object's current score when the event ended 0 to 1 area REAL Frigate. Width × height of the object's box, in pixels ratio REAL Frigate. Width ÷ height of the object's box Less than 1 is taller than wide motionless_count REAL Frigate. Frames in which the object didn't move A count position_changes REAL Frigate. How many times the object changed position A count attributes TEXT Frigate. Attributes detected on the object, with their best scores A JSON object, such as {"face": 0.86}; usually empty direction_calc TEXT Direction of travel relative to the device outbound (away from the device), inbound (toward it), or empty. See Direction and speed. speed_calc REAL Speed from the radar, in the radar's units (mph by default) Positive for inbound and negative for outbound; empty if no speed was matched provenance TEXT Which sensors contributed, primary first A JSON array: ["frigate"], or ["frigate", "radar"] when a speed was matched radarName TEXT The radar paired with the camera, if that radar is enabled, whether or not it supplied a speed A radar name such as TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00, or empty deployment_id TEXT Where the device was. See the deployment table. A deployment.id, or empty

docs.title: MQTT and ThingsBoard
docs.text: The MQTT broker is on by default and accepts connections only from the device itself. The ThingsBoard upload is off until you turn it on.

docs.title: MQTT
docs.text:
Node-RED hosts an MQTT broker on the device at port 1883. Frigate, the air quality sensor, and Node-RED connect to it on the device. Other devices on your network, such as Home Assistant or a display board that shows the day's counts, can connect once you give the broker a login; see Connect from other devices. Settings are in node-red-tm.env.

Topic Direction Contents frigate/events Frigate to the Traffic Monitor Frigate's event messages. The Traffic Monitor records the ones with type: "end" as events. frigate/<camera>/<object>/snapshot Frigate to subscribers A cropped JPEG of each detected object, which can show a person. Frigate publishes it only when the camera's mqtt setting is on, and new installs turn it off. The Traffic Monitor doesn't use it. See Tune object detection. aq/<sensor>/readings Air quality sensor to the Traffic Monitor One JSON reading. See Air quality. tm/events The Traffic Monitor to subscribers Today's cumulative counts, mainly for a display board. Published with QoS 1 and retained, so a new subscriber gets the latest counts at once. See below.

tm/event, without the s, is the per-event message inside Node-RED. Each recorded event carries it to the dashboards and to the ThingsBoard upload. It isn't published on the broker, so MQTT clients such as Home Assistant can't subscribe to it.

docs.title: tm/events
docs.text:
A JSON object with the same counts as Today's counts on the Monitoring dashboard: events that passed through zone_capture, for the camera selected on the legacy dashboard at http://<device>/ui/, in a day that starts at 04:00 local time.

Key Meaning car, person, bicycle, motorcycle, bus, dog, ... One key per object type that has been counted today, named as Frigate labels it bicycle_adj bicycle plus motorcycle. Present once a bicycle has been counted. person_adj person minus bicycle minus motorcycle: a pedestrian count, because every cyclist is also detected as a person. Scooter riders count as people. It can be negative, when more bicycles and motorcycles than people have been counted. Present once a person has been counted. event_latest The object type of the most recent counted event, such as car

To watch it from another computer:

mosquitto_sub -h <device> -u <username> -P <password> -t tm/events

docs.title: Connect from other devices
docs.text:
1. Give the broker a login:

    bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm -C mqtt_lan

    This creates the username tm and a random password. To choose your own instead, set TM_MQTT_BROKER_USERNAME and TM_MQTT_BROKER_PASSWORD in /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/node-red-tm.env and run the command without -C mqtt_lan. Use only letters, digits, ., _, and -, with no quotes and no comment after the value on the same line; otherwise the installer stops with a message.

    The broker then requires the login from every client, the installer gives it to Frigate, and port 1883 opens to your network.

  2. Read the login:

    sudo grep ^TM_MQTT_BROKER_ /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/node-red-tm.env

  3. Give it to the air quality sensor and to each MQTT client.

  4. Check from another computer:

    mosquitto_sub -h <device> -u <username> -P <password> -t tm/events

  5. To change the login, edit the two values and run bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm again. To remove it, leave both values blank and run the same command: the broker stops checking logins and port 1883 closes to the network.

Warning

The login crosses the network unencrypted, and anyone who has it can read every topic and publish false data. Open MQTT only on a network you trust.

docs.title: ThingsBoard
docs.text:
The device can upload its data to a ThingsBoard server, which gives you dashboards and storage for a fleet of devices. Turn it on in the thingsboard section of config.yml with the server's hostname, and enter the device's access token on the control app's Device page. Saving the token restarts Node-RED, which takes about thirty seconds. The device picks up a change to the file when you save it.

Once connected, the device sends over ThingsBoard's HTTP API:

  • Each event as telemetry, with ts set to the event's frame_time in milliseconds and values holding every column of the event.
  • Each radar and air quality reading as telemetry. Readings from the high-rate radar tables are batched to avoid hundreds of messages per vehicle.
  • The device's system metrics as telemetry, every five minutes.
  • The deployment location, radar information, and the Traffic Monitor settings as device attributes.

docs.title: Config backup
docs.text: With ThingsBoard connected, the Backup & Restore section of the legacy dashboard at http://<device>/ui/ saves Frigate's config as an attribute of the device in ThingsBoard.

docs.title: description: The five radar tables: detected object velocities, timed counts, raw speed and magnitude readings, and per-object summaries.
Radar
docs.text:
The OmniPreSense OPS243-A Doppler radar measures the speed and direction of whatever moves in front of it, does its own signal processing, and reports readings over USB as JSON. The Traffic Monitor turns on several of the radar's reporting modes when the service starts and whenever config.yml is saved, and stores each kind of reading in its own table. The radar's API guide describes the modes and the commands.

Reading Radar command Table What it is Detected object velocity ON radar_dov The radar decides an object is present when it sees two consecutive speed reports, then reports the highest speed, and again if a higher one follows. One or a few readings per object. These readings supply the speeds for events. Timed speed counts @O, every 300 seconds radar_timed_speed_counts How many objects passed in each direction during the interval, and their average speed Raw speed and magnitude OS and OM with O3 radar_raw_speed_magnitude The three strongest speed and magnitude pairs from each sample. Magnitude reflects the object's size, distance, and reflectivity. Strongest reading the first of the three above radar_raw_speed_magnitude_single The single strongest pair from each sample, for easier analysis Object summary OC radar_oc_payload One row per object, with its time in view, speed range, magnitude, and estimated length. Needs OPS9243 firmware.

Across the tables, direction is inbound (toward the radar) or outbound (away from it), speeds are positive for inbound and negative for outbound, and the unit is the radar's speed unit, mph by default. radarName is the radar's name from config.yml, and deployment_id points at the deployment the reading was taken in.

The times come from the radar's own clock, which starts again from zero whenever the radar loses power. The Traffic Monitor sets that clock from the device's clock when the service starts, whenever config.yml is saved, every hour, and within about half a minute of a radar being plugged back in.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Thank you for your interest in getting involved! We welcome all skill levels and abilities as contributions. Visit our Traffic Monitor GitHub page to get involved.

Contributions can include any of the following plus more!

  • 💡 Feature requests and use case ideas
  • 🐞 Bug reports
  • 👩‍💻 Code contributions, see Contributing
  • 👍 Comment on or thumbs-up milestones or issues
  • 💬 Questions, comments, and videos/images of your deployments on our Traffic Monitor Zulip Chat!

We foster a safe and welcoming community, review our Code of Conduct.

docs.title: Use of AI tools
docs.text: You may use AI coding assistants to help draft, review, or explain a contribution, but you remain its author: understand and test every change you submit. Never share images, video clips, or plate reads with an AI tool, and use placeholders instead of real passwords, keys, or tokens. The de-identified tmdb.sqlite database may be shared only with the device operator's explicit consent, and never if plate recognition was ever enabled, because it then holds plate numbers. See Use of AI tools in CONTRIBUTING.md for the details and for how to label AI-assisted commits.

docs.title: Writing docs
docs.text:
These docs are Markdown files in the repo's docs/ folder, built with Material for MkDocs. Docs changes go in the same pull request as the code they describe, against dev.

  • Preview while you edit: from the repo root, run python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/tm-docs && ~/.venvs/tm-docs/bin/pip install --require-hashes -r docs-site/requirements.txt once, then ~/.venvs/tm-docs/bin/mkdocs serve and open http://127.0.0.1:8000.
  • Check before you push: mkdocs build --strict fails on broken links, anchors, and images, and on pages missing from the nav. Pull requests run the same check.
  • New pages go in the nav: list in mkdocs.yml, under the section for the reader's job (see below). A page outside the folders already listed under the llmstxt plugin also goes in that plugin's matching section, so AI tools can find it in llms.txt. Keep a page's file path when you move it in the nav; if the path must change, add the old path to the moved map in docs-site/pages-root/404.html.
  • Images go in docs/assets/images/. Link them with Markdown, ![Alt text](../assets/images/name.png), so the build can check the path. Add a caption with <figure markdown="span"> (see existing pages).
  • Callouts use admonitions: !!! info, !!! success, !!! warning, or !!! danger, followed by the text indented four spaces.

Versions: pushes to dev publish to /dev/, and each release tag (vX.Y.Z) publishes a frozen copy and becomes /latest/, the default version.

docs.title: Style
docs.text:
Aim for pages that are complete but quick to read: everything the reader needs, and nothing they don't. These rules apply to every docs change, whether a person or an AI tool drafted it.

  • One reader and one job per page. Pages about installing, setup, configuration, the dashboards, and the data tell the person running a device what to do or what something means. Details for contributors go in the Development pages or in the README next to the code. Diátaxis names the four jobs: tutorial, how-to guide, reference, and explanation. Use it to decide what belongs on the page you're editing, not to reorganize the site. The nav sections map to those jobs:

    Section Job Reader Get started Explanation and orientation Anyone new Build your own, Deploy, Add-ons How-to guides, one task per page Someone building or installing a device Use the device How-to guides for the running device Someone operating a device Reference Tables: every setting, flag, topic, and column Someone looking a value up Ideas and use cases, Help Ideas, troubleshooting, and where to ask Someone curious or stuck Development Contributors You * Leave out what the reader won't act on, such as Ansible variables and task names, Node-RED node names, and files they won't open. Give real values, such as the default install folder /opt/traffic-monitor, instead of variables. * Revise in place. Rewrite the text your change affects and delete what it makes obsolete, rather than adding a paragraph. Keep the docs edit in proportion to the change; a diff that removes more than it adds is fine. * Describe how things work, not how they changed. Don't narrate changes ("now supports", "new in", "previously"). Each release has its own copy of the docs, and history belongs in commit messages and release notes. * Say each fact once, and link to it from other pages. Link to config files and code in the repo instead of copying them into a page, because copies go stale. Link to the main branch, which tracks the latest release, so the link matches /latest/ rather than /dev/. * Put the common case first. Move edge cases and troubleshooting into a collapsed callout (??? instead of !!!), a table, or the FAQ. * Use tables for reference data, with one row per setting or database column and its type, default, and meaning. * Keep the language plain: "you", present tense, active voice, short sentences, and no filler such as "simply", "just", or "note that". Save callouts for what the reader must not miss. * Check every value against the code, including defaults, paths, ports, and names.

For anything these rules don't cover, follow the Google developer documentation style guide.

docs.title: description: Set up to change the Traffic Monitor: the Node-RED flows, the database schema, and testing on a dev Pi.
Dev environment
docs.text:
The Traffic Monitor is open source, so you can change your devices to suit your needs. If others would benefit, join the community and contribute back.

The repository is a monorepo with everything needed to run a device: the installer, the container definitions, the Node-RED flows, and these docs.

docs.title: Node-RED logic
docs.text:
Node-RED runs the Traffic Monitor's logic: it receives events from Frigate and readings from the radar, pairs events with speeds, writes the database, serves the dashboards, and sends data on. The flows are in the repository at container/node-red-tm/data/flows.json, and the installer copies them to the device on every run, so changes made only in a device's editor are lost on the next update.

To develop on a device:

  1. Log in to the device as the administrator, then open the Node-RED editor at http://<device>/nr/. The editor has no login of its own.
  2. Create a new project and clone your fork of the repository. This replaces the flows on the device, so save any changes first.
  3. Point the project's flow and package files at container/node-red-tm/data/flows.json and package.json, so your edits land in the repository's files.
  4. Commit your changes to a branch of your fork.
  5. Open a pull request, following Contributing.

docs.title: Database schema
docs.text:
The tables are defined by numbered SQL migrations in container/node-red-tm/schema/migrations/, not by the flows. Each time node-red-tm.service starts, it applies the migrations the database doesn't have yet, before Node-RED opens it. The README.md in the schema directory describes the whole process, from writing a migration to testing the upgrade on a Pi.

To change the schema:

  1. Add the next numbered migration, regenerate schema.sql, and update the table docs under Data.

  2. Run the tests, using the dev environment from Contributing:

    .venv/bin/python -m pytest container/node-red-tm/schema/tests

To try a migration on a dev device, apply it while Node-RED is stopped. Deploying from the Node-RED editor doesn't restart the service, so it doesn't apply migrations. These commands use the default owner (tmadmin) and install folder, and run the migration script from your Node-RED project's clone:

sudo systemctl stop node-red-tm.service
sudo runuser -u tmadmin -- python3 \
    /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/data/projects/<project>/container/node-red-tm/schema/tmdb_migrate.py \
    --db /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/db/tmdb.sqlite
sudo systemctl start node-red-tm.service

The database records each migration it applies. If you change a migration after applying it, restore the copy saved in /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/db/backup/ and apply it again.

docs.title: Control app
docs.text: The control app in tm-control/ serves the home page and the login in front of every app. tm-control describes its code, how the login reaches each app, and how to run it on a laptop without a Pi.

docs.title: Testing on a dev Pi
docs.text:
script/devpi/tmdev.py deploys your working copy to a bench Pi over SSH, runs commands on it, and records a PR's Pi test plan as a checklist. Every deploy, command, and check goes into a run log on your machine, so you can see later what ran on which Pi and how it went.

The Pis are defined in an inventory file that lists each Pi's address, login, and SSH key, plus the hardware it should have. That file and the run log stay on your machine, outside the repository. script/devpi/README.md covers setup and use.

Warning

Use these tools only with bench units, not field devices. Deploys pass -y to the installer, so the Pi reboots whenever the installer needs it.

docs.title: description: How the control app (tm-control) is built: its backend modules, the login check nginx runs for every app, the status checks, root jobs and polkit, fake mode, and how to add a module or a check.
tm-control
docs.text:
tm-control is the device's control app: the home page, setup, the login in front of every app, the device's accounts, and the Status, Device, Date and time, Detection, and Location pages. Control app and login, Check and fix the device, Choose the detection model, and Places and location describe it from the operator's side. This page is for changing it.

It has three parts, all in the repository's tm-control/ folder:

Folder What it is How it reaches the device backend/ The Python app (FastAPI) and the tm-control command Copied root-owned to /usr/local/lib/traffic-monitor/tm-control, with its own virtual environment, and run as tm-control.service ui/ The web pages (Vue 3, Vuetify 3, TypeScript, Vite) Built into the reverse proxy's image and served by nginx at / jobs/ Scripts for the few things that need root Copied root-owned to /usr/local/libexec/traffic-monitor/ and run by fixed systemd units

docs.title: How it runs
docs.text:
tm-control.service runs on the host, not in the pod, so the login keeps working when Podman doesn't. It runs as the code owner (default tmadmin), never as root, in a systemd sandbox, and listens on 127.0.0.1:8090 only. nginx is the only way in from the network.

It reads two things the installer writes, and keeps one database of its own:

  • /etc/traffic-monitor/secrets/: two kinds of secret. Five are generated once on the device: the session key, Frigate's proxy secret, the Node-RED editor's token key, the token for Node-RED's internal status, and go2rtc's RTSP password. Four are entered by an administrator: the ThingsBoard access token and the Plate Recognizer token and license key on the Device page, and the Frigate+ API key on the Detection page. The installer creates them empty, and only the set-secret job writes them. GENERATED_SECRETS and ENTERED_SECRETS in core/secrets.py match the role's tmsetup_secret_names and tmsetup_entered_secret_names (a test keeps each pair equal), DEVICE_SECRETS is the two together, and the diagnostics redact the value of each. An empty file means the secret isn't set. The secrets module (GET /secrets, and POST and DELETE /secrets/{name}) lists what is set, never a value, and starts the job.
  • /etc/traffic-monitor/manifest.json: what the installer installed and found, such as the version, the installing user, the proxied apps, the home page's colors, and, on a device with a Coral, the model section the installer gives Frigate (frigate.coral_model, from the role's tmsetup_frigate_coral_model), which the Detection page puts back, and network, the hotspot's Wi-Fi device, profile name, and address (wlan0, tm-hotspot, 10.42.0.1, from the role's tmsetup_wifi_device, tmsetup_hotspot_profile, and tmsetup_hotspot_address), which the Network checks and tm-control card read.
  • /var/lib/tm-control/state.sqlite: users, the claim and the setup code's hash, license acceptances, job records, an audit log, and the Location page's places (surveys, survey_bearings, and survey_corrections). Numbered migrations in core/state.py create and update it, recorded in PRAGMA user_version. Never change a migration that has shipped; add the next one.

While the device is unclaimed, the installer keeps the setup code in a root-only file, /etc/traffic-monitor/setup-code, and hands it to tm-control set-setup-code on every run, which stores only its hash. The installer's command-line steps run as the code owner, and sudo tm-control reset-admin drops to that user after writing a new code file, so root never writes the database.

docs.title: The login check
docs.text:
nginx checks every app path with auth_request before it proxies the request. Each app's location file includes one of two snippets, auth-viewer.conf (any logged-in user) or auth-admin.conf (administrators), which send a subrequest to tm-control's GET /api/v1/auth/verify:

browser ──GET /frigate/──▶ nginx (port 80)
                             │  auth_request /_auth  (internal location)
                             │    X-Original-URI: /frigate/
                             │    X-TM-Required-Role: viewer   (admin for /_auth_admin)
                             │    X-Forwarded-For: the browser's address
                             │    Cookie: tm_session=…
                             ▼
                           tm-control 127.0.0.1:8090  /api/v1/auth/verify
                             │
       ┌─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
       ▼                     ▼                          ▼                          ▼
  200 + identity       401 + X-TM-Redirect         403 forbidden        no answer (down, timeout)
  headers               (/setup, /login?next=…,     nginx returns 403    nginx returns 503 with
       │                 /welcome, or /waiting)                          the rescue page
       │                nginx answers 302
       ▼
  nginx proxies to the app, adding the headers that app needs

A 200 carries X-TM-User, X-TM-Role, X-TM-Frigate-Secret, and, for administrators, X-TM-NR-Token. The snippets copy them into nginx variables, and each app's location passes on what that app understands:

App What nginx sends it Frigate (127.0.0.1:8971) X-Forwarded-User and X-Forwarded-Groups (the role), and X-Proxy-Secret, which Frigate checks against FRIGATE_PROXY_AUTH_SECRET in frigate.env. nginx always sends both forwarded headers, because Frigate serves a request with only the secret as its default role, and it blanks Remote-User, Remote-Groups, and Remote-Role, which Frigate would also trust. Frigate's own login is off (auth: enabled: false). Node-RED editor (/nr/) x-tm-nr-token, a short-lived token that settings.js checks with TM_NR_TOKEN_KEY from node-red-tm.env. The editor has no users of its own. Dashboards, camera feeds, Cockpit, data downloads No identity: nginx's check is the whole gate. Cockpit then asks for its own Raspberry Pi login.

A few rules keep the check sound:

  • Only nginx's internal /_auth and /_auth_admin locations may call verify. A location ^~ /api/v1/auth/verify returns 404 to the network, the /api/ location clears X-TM-Required-Role, and verify answers 404 without that header.
  • The check is always a GET without a body, and without the Authorization header, so Cockpit's Basic login never reaches tm-control.
  • Sessions last 7 days and roll: verify and the API re-issue a cookie that's more than a day old, and the snippets pass verify's Set-Cookie on to the browser. An app location must not set an add_header of its own, or it would drop that cookie.
  • Only the check's own failure, which auth_request turns into a 500, becomes the rescue page (error_page 500 =503 /unavailable.html). An app's own 502 or 504 stays as it is.

The Node-RED token is base64url(JSON {"u", "r", "exp"}), a dot, and base64url(HMAC-SHA256(key, first part)), without padding, valid for 5 minutes. NodeRedToken in backend/tm_control/core/auth.py mints it, and verifyProxyToken in container/node-red-tm/data/settings.js checks it. Change both together; script/tests/test_node_red_settings.py runs tokens from one through the other.

The rest of the API, under /api/v1/, checks the session cookie itself. Every error has one shape, {"error": {"code", "message", "detail"}}. A request that changes something must send JSON from a page on the device (a matching Origin or Referer), or it gets 403.

docs.title: Download links
docs.text:
Android's sign-in window, which on Android 17 is the only browser that can reach a unit on its hotspot, fetches a download twice: its own request carries the session cookie, then it hands the address to a download helper that sends no cookie. So the Data export page asks for a link that passes the check once without the cookie:

  1. Just before it starts a download, the page sends POST /api/v1/auth/download-link with {"files": …}. tm-control answers an administrator with /storefiles?files=…&tm_token=…, a random one-time token kept in memory. Anyone else gets an error, and the page falls back to the plain /storefiles?files=… address, which still works wherever the browser downloads the file itself.
  2. The browser's own request has a session, so verify checks it as usual and leaves the link unused.
  3. The helper's request has no session. verify lets it through as the administrator only when the address is exactly /storefiles with files and tm_token and nothing else, on an admin location, within 600 seconds, from the address the link was made for (X-Forwarded-For, which the /_auth locations set to nginx's own $remote_addr), and for the same files. The user must still be an administrator with the same sessions, and the current license agreement must be accepted. The answer carries X-TM-User and X-TM-Role only: no Frigate secret, no Node-RED token, no cookie.

The first request without a session that presents a token spends it, whether or not the rest matched. A login redirect leaves the token out of its next=. nginx's access log records the token; the parameter is named tm_token so that the diagnostics download hides its value with every other key ending in token. The two download templates live in flows.json (the ui-templates "Button to trigger download request" and "redirect to storefiles URL"), and script/tests/test_node_red_flows.py checks that they ask for the same link.

docs.title: Backend layout
docs.text:
tm-control/backend/tm_control/
  app.py         create_app(): loads the state, secrets, manifest, and license agreement, and mounts the modules
  cli.py         the tm-control command: serve, migrate, claim-status, set-setup-code, reset-admin, card,
                 and for development fake-reset and dump-openapi
  fake.py        fake mode's reset and the OpenAPI dump
  core/          shared rules: auth (passwords, sessions, backoff, setup code, users), csrf, errors, jobs,
                 card (the device's card), manifest, migrate (config updates for older installs), secrets, settings, state
  adapters/      the outside world: command (runs an argv list with a timeout and an output cap, never a shell),
                 systemd, timedate, sysinfo, hardware, network (nmcli and iw, read-only), the apps' HTTP APIs (frigate,
                 nodered, go2rtc), mqtt,
                 redact, yamlfile
  modules/       one folder per feature, each with a router: auth, setup, account, jobs, status, services, apps,
                 hardware, network, secrets, system, time, detection, location

Rules live in the backend; the UI shows what the API returns and posts what the operator types. tm-control/ui/README.md describes the UI's layout and design.

docs.title: Root jobs and polkit
docs.text:
tm-control never runs as root and never uses sudo. polkit lets its user do two things, both listed in tmsetup_tm_control_polkit in the role's vars/main.yml, and nothing else:

  • Start, stop, and restart a fixed list of units. tm-control itself isn't on it; restart it with Cockpit or SSH. tm-network-retry.service is on it for the Hotspot check's fix, and FIX_UNITS in modules/services/units.py lists the units like it, which a check's fix may start but the Services list doesn't show; POST /services/{unit}/restart accepts them.
  • Seven actions: org.freedesktop.timedate1.set-time, set-timezone, and set-ntp for the Date and time page, and org.freedesktop.login1.reboot, reboot-multiple-sessions, power-off, and power-off-multiple-sessions for the Device page. The -ignore-inhibit variants aren't granted, so tm-control asks logind (CanReboot, CanPowerOff) first and answers 409 while an inhibitor, such as an update, holds the device up.

A time zone change restarts traffic-monitor.service and revproxy.service after the response, because the containers bind-mount /etc/localtime and keep the old zone until they restart. A time change that moved the clock ahead by more than 20 seconds (FRIGATE_JUMP_SECONDS in modules/time/router.py), by set-time or by NTP while the request watched, restarts frigate.service the same way, or at once when a later step of the request fails. Frigate's capture stops on such a step and, from a few minutes, may not recover by itself. A time zone change in the same request restarts the pod instead, which covers Frigate. Each admin action records an audit row. For work that needs root, tm-control writes a request to /run/tm-control/jobs/<name>.json and starts tm-job-<name>.service, a fixed root-owned oneshot unit. Its script in tm-control/jobs/ checks the request strictly, does one thing, and deletes the request. tm-control follows the run through the unit and the journal, and GET /api/v1/jobs/{id} reports its status and log lines. There are two jobs:

Job What it does system-password Sets the installing user's Linux password. It refuses an account that doesn't exist or has uid 0. tmsetup.sh also refuses to run as root, but a remote install with -l root still records root as the installing user, so the job's own check is the one that counts. set-secret Writes or empties one entered secret. The request holds the secret's name and value. The script accepts only the four names in its own table (thingsboard_access_token, frigate_plus_api_key, plate_recognizer_token, and plate_recognizer_license_key), and only an empty value or one that matches that secret's pattern, and it refuses anything else without printing the value. It writes the secret's file, rewrites the secret's KEY= lines in node-red-tm.env, frigate.env, or plate-recognizer.env, then restarts the units that read them, in that order. A step that fails leaves the device no worse than before, and the log says which step it was. If a restart fails, the secret is already written, and the next Save runs again.

SECRETS in tm-control/jobs/tm-job-set-secret repeats the secrets' patterns (VALUE_PATTERNS in core/secrets.py) and restart units (ENTERED in modules/secrets/router.py), because the script imports nothing from tm-control; tests keep them the same.

docs.title: Status checks
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/status returns a report of check groups, which the Status page shows and the home page sums up in one line. Each module lists its groups in Module.check_groups, and the report shows them in MODULES order: Services, Apps, Configuration (the apps module's second group), Hardware, Network, Device (from the system module), and Date and time.

A check function takes a Context and returns a list of Checks, each with an id, a title, a status (ok, warn, error, or unknown), a one- or two-sentence detail that says what to do, and an optional fix:

Fix kind The UI shows restart A button, for admins, that restarts unit after a confirmation. Make it with restart_fix() in modules/services/units.py, so every such button reads Restart <unit title>. rescan One "Re-scan hardware" button at the end of the group, for admins, which calls POST /status/rescan. link A link to href, a page in the UI such as /time or /device. hint text, after the detail.

The runner in core/checks.py keeps the page up whatever a probe does:

  • Checks never raise. A function that raises, or doesn't finish within the group's 5-second timeout, becomes one unknown check that names the exception class or the timeout, never its message, which could hold a command's output or a secret.
  • All groups run at the same time, so a hung app costs about one timeout, not one per check.
  • Context.probe(key, fn) runs fn once per report for every check that asks for the same key. Frigate's config and stats, Node-RED's status, config.yml, the unit states, and the bus listings are each read once.
  • The report is cached for 5 seconds; POST /status/rescan (admins) runs it again at once.

Details name cameras, zones, radars, units, and config keys, never a URL, a password, or a command's output. The one exception is Frigate's log, which two checks quote:

  • The Apps group's Frigate check is an error when /api/config says safe_mode: true (probes.frigate_safe_mode), which is how Frigate answers a config that doesn't validate: it starts with no cameras, so config.cameras, config.zones, apps.frigate.cameras, and apps.go2rtc.streams have nothing to compare, report unknown, and point at this check. The detail quotes Frigate's validation messages.
  • The Configuration group's Frigate+ check (config.frigate_plus) reads model.path from Frigate's config.yml on disk, whether the frigate_plus_api_key secret is set, and whether a plus:// model's two files are in model_cache. It warns about a key without a plus:// model, and is an error for a plus:// model Frigate can't get or can't use, quoting the log line that says why. Whenever Frigate doesn't answer, whatever systemd says of the unit (in a crash loop it's active between crashes), it quotes the traceback's last line without claiming the download caused it, because the journal's tail shows how Frigate stopped, not why; with no such line it's unknown. When that line holds Frigate's Unable to refresh API token (REFUSED_KEY), which Frigate raises for any answer but a token, the detail says Frigate+ gave no token for the key, as with a wrong key or an unreachable Frigate+, and links to the key form; both errors end with the ways out in WAYS_OUT. When the model's two files are on the device, Frigate loads it without asking Frigate+, so the detail quotes the line without the fetch advice and points at the Apps group's Frigate check. That check quotes the same line, with a link to the diagnostics and a pointer to the Services row's restart, since a crash loop without a plus:// model has no other check to name its cause. probes.frigate_journal reads the current run's messages while the unit is active and either Frigate answers or systemd hasn't restarted it after a failure, and the journal's tail otherwise, where the run that failed left its traceback. A failure restart is NRestarts above 0 whose last automatic restart didn't follow Frigate's own exit 143 (units.last_restart_cause, from PID 1's journal, as the Services group reads it): after a Save & Restart the counter is 1 while Frigate starts, and the run before the save mustn't be quoted. One of Frigate's own restarts within RESTART_LOOP_SPACING (120 s) of the counted automatic restart before it is a loop, not a save (units.restart_causes, from PID 1's restart times alone; a hand restart resets the count, so a single restart is never a loop): the Services row warns with the counts, the Apps group's Frigate check says Frigate keeps stopping itself while it isn't answering, and the probe reads the tail. The restart Frigate's watchdog makes when a detector process dies is the known case; tm-control reads no log line for it.

Both quote only the Message : lines of Frigate's validation block and the last line of a traceback, through redact() in modules/apps/checks.py, which replaces anything shaped like a Frigate+ key with <key> and cuts each line to MESSAGE_MAX characters. traceback_last_line strips journalctl's prefix and the timestamp Frigate's s6 supervisor puts on each line (S6_TIMESTAMP) before it matches an exception line. It quotes nothing when s6's [INFO] Service Frigate exited with code 0 line (ORDERLY_EXIT; a kill by SIGTERM counts too) comes after the last exception line. Frigate logs two tracebacks of its own while it stops for a Save & Restart, and the unit stays active until its container has halted, so the probe reads the run that is stopping; a crash of Frigate's own process has a nonzero exit line, so that crash loop still quotes; Frigate's watchdog restarts it the same way as a save when a detector process dies, so that loop quotes nothing, and is caught by its cadence instead.

The Hardware group's accelerator check claims only the host side ("Ready on the host and passed to Frigate"). Frigate's stats keep a dead detector process's pid and its starting 10.0 ms, so whether detection works is Frigate's to report, through the restarts above.

docs.title: Add a check
docs.text:
1. Write the function in the module's checks.py. Read through context.probe anything another check also reads, and run commands through adapters/command.run with an argv list, a timeout of at most 4 seconds, and an output cap. HTTP reads go to 127.0.0.1 only, with a 3-second timeout.
  2. Add it to the module's CheckGroup, or make a new group and list it in the module's check_groups.
  3. Test each status it can return, with synthetic data. The backend tests' device_client fixture builds the app as on a device (fake mode off, synthetic secrets, the test manifest), with the apps not answering and the hardware absent, so an API test runs the real code with only the outside world stubbed.
  4. Add the check to tests/fixtures/status_fake.json if fake mode should show a new status or kind of fix.

docs.title: Node-RED's internal status
docs.text: Node-RED answers GET /tm-internal/status on 127.0.0.1:1880 with its uptime, the errors from its last config.yml load, the database's schema version, and each radar's port and last reading. A flow on the init-config tab serves it. It checks the X-TM-Internal-Token header against TM_INTERNAL_TOKEN in node-red-tm.env, which the installer fills from the node_red_internal_token secret on every run, and refuses every request when that variable is unset or empty. adapters/nodered.py reads it, and calls the Location module's endpoints on the same port with the same token (see The Location module). nginx answers 404 for /nr/tm-internal/ in any letter case, because Node-RED matches paths whatever their case. The JSON fields are a contract between the flow and the checks: script/tests/test_node_red_flows.py and tests/fixtures/nodered_status.json pin them.

docs.title: The Detection module
docs.text:
The detection module serves the Detection page. It reads Frigate's running config and config.yml, and the files in Frigate's model_cache. Its routes, under /api/v1/models:

Route Who What it does GET /models Any logged-in user The detector, the running model, the models in model_cache with their files, hashes, and each one's labels, and the two label lists for the running model PUT /models/upload/{filename} Admin Streams a model file, a sidecar, or a zip or tar.gz of both into model_cache POST /models/{name}/sidecar Admin Writes the sidecar for a model file that has none, from the form's values POST /models/{name}/use Admin Sets Frigate's model: section to the model, then restarts Frigate POST /models/default/use Admin Puts back the installer's model, or removes the section on a device without a Coral GET /models/{name}/package Admin A zip of the model's two files and SHA256SUMS GET /models/{name}/file Admin The model file alone, for a model with no sidecar to package, such as the installer's DELETE /models/{name} Admin Removes the model's files, unless it runs or is the installer's or Frigate's own default

The module writes only inside model_cache and Frigate's config.yml, plus its own state directory. Every model_cache write goes through a descriptor of the directory opened with O_NOFOLLOW, after valid_name has checked the name; config.yml is edited by its path through RoundTripFile, as tm-control migrate edits config files (a backup, an atomic replace, the owner kept). When Frigate answers in safe mode, which it enters when its config fails to validate, it runs a stand-in config, so GET /models reads the detector and the running model from config.yml and says frigate_safe_mode; a Use still goes through Frigate's API, which validates the whole config. The caps are 100 MB for a request and a model file, 2 MB for a sidecar, 3 archive members, and 512 MB of free storage left afterwards. Use goes through Frigate's config API, which checks the whole config, and edits config.yml itself, with a backup, only when Frigate doesn't answer. Both end in a restart of frigate.service.

Uploads need two things from the edge. nginx has its own location, ^~ /api/v1/models/upload/ in tm-control-api.conf.j2, with client_max_body_size 100m and proxy_request_buffering off, so the body streams to tm-control instead of being buffered. Because of that, tm-control reads the rest of a refused upload before it answers, so nginx can pass the answer on rather than a 502. The upload body is application/octet-stream, which the cross-site check in core/csrf.py admits along with application/json, because the check still requires a same-origin request. Every other /api/ path keeps nginx's default body limit.

The sidecars are a Frigate+ model record's JSON. The module reads only the fields the page shows and keeps the whole file as it was uploaded, so a download returns it unchanged. It never puts a record's other fields in an answer, a log line, or an audit row.

docs.title: The Location module
docs.text:
The location module serves the Location page. It's for admins only, because the places hold exact coordinates: every route under /api/v1/surveys takes require_admin. The places are in state.sqlite; the place in use is also in Node-RED's config.yml, under deployment:, which is what Node-RED reads. tm-control never opens tmdb.sqlite, and Node-RED never opens state.sqlite.

Route What it does GET /surveys The place in use, the precision, the enabled sensors and their bearings, the places with Node-RED's usage counts, and the deployments recorded before any place. Runs the reconcile first. POST /surveys, PATCH and DELETE /surveys/{id} Plan a place, edit a planned one, delete one that isn't in use POST /surveys/{id}/deploy Writes the place and every enabled sensor's bearing into config.yml, then asks Node-RED every second, for up to 20 seconds, for the new deployments. reloaded: false when they didn't appear, which isn't an error: the file is written. PUT /surveys/precision Writes database_precision; with round_stored, also has Node-RED round the rows already stored POST /surveys/{id}/location, POST /surveys/{id}/deployments/{deployment_id}/bearing Corrections: the place's point, re-rounded in Node-RED's rows, or one deployment's bearing; each records a row in survey_corrections GET /surveys/{id}/deployments, GET /surveys/{id}/events A place's deployments, and its event count and span, from Node-RED POST /surveys/import Planned places from a CSV: a dry run lists what it read, and the import creates all or none

The rules:

  • coordinates.py holds them: survey ids (<8 hex>-si, from secrets.token_hex(4)), typed coordinates quantised to five decimal places half away from zero on their decimal text, and the stored ones rounded half away from zero, as SQLite's ROUND and the flows' toFixed do. The UI's coordinates.ts only checks a pasted pair before it sends; the API's answer wins.
  • config.py edits config.yml through RoundTripFile, with mapping_indent=4, so comments, key order, and quoting stay. Each save keeps a backup beside the file, of which the newest 10 stay, and replaces it atomically. The backups of Frigate's config.yml from the Detection page's file fallback follow the same limit. Pruning touches only these config.yml.<UTC stamp>.bak names. It leaves the Ansible backups from tmsetup.sh, a copy made by hand, and every <file>.<UTC stamp>.migrate.bak from tm-control migrate, which can hold the only copy of what the migration removed. A file changed since it was read is a ConcurrentEditError, which the API answers with 409 config_changed.
  • reconcile.py keeps the store and the file in step. It runs at claim, on every GET /surveys, and before the checks of every status report that isn't the cached one (StatusCache's prepare), under app.state.reconcile_lock, which every write also holds. The status report waits at most two seconds for that lock, skips the run when a write holds it longer, and logs any error by its class name. Once per device it makes the first place: on a fresh device (no coordinates, no survey_id, and no backup), First location with no coordinates; on an upgraded one, a used place for each survey in the newest tmdb-v0-* or tmdb-v1-* backup in node-red-tm/db/backup/, opened read-only and immutable, then the place in use from the file. It waits until Node-RED reports schema version 2. An unreadable backup is skipped with one log line. Every run after that follows hand edits of the file, as Edit the location by hand describes.
  • No coordinate, description, or reason is logged, audited, or put in an error message. Audit rows carry the survey id, and a deployment id or the precision.

The module calls six Node-RED endpoints, besides /tm-internal/status, on 127.0.0.1:1880 with X-TM-Internal-Token. Flows on the init-config tab serve them, and script/tests/test_node_red_flows.py pins them:

Endpoint What it does GET /tm-internal/deployments?survey_id=<id> A survey's deployment rows GET /tm-internal/surveys/usage First start, last end, and open and total deployment counts for each survey, and for the rows with no survey GET /tm-internal/surveys/<id>/events A survey's event count, and its first and last event POST /tm-internal/deployments/precision Rounds every stored row to a coarser precision, or clears the coordinates for none POST /tm-internal/surveys/<id>/location Rewrites a survey's stored coordinates from a new point, each row at its own precision POST /tm-internal/deployments/<id>/bearing Rewrites one deployment's bearing

tm-control migrate --node-red-config, run by the installer, also brings deployment: up to date: it adds database_precision: '2' where it's missing, and removes lat and lon from a sensor's own deployment: block. The Location check (location in modules/apps/contracts.py) checks the same keys at run time.

docs.title: The Network module and the hotspot
docs.text:
The network module has no routes yet. It adds the Network check group (hotspot, wifi, internet, and wifi_country, in modules/network/checks.py), read-only through adapters/network.py, which runs nmcli and iw and never asks for a secret. An offline unit is normal, so the Internet check is never a warning or an error, and a read that fails is unknown. The hotspot's values come from the manifest's network section. The checks' words are the contract with the operator page.

Two scripts in jobs/ run as root, and neither is a tm-job unit. Both are standard-library Python with no tm_control imports, run as /usr/bin/python3 -EP from the root-owned /usr/local/libexec/traffic-monitor/, and read no password into their output:

Script Run by What it does tm-hotspot-setup The installer's wifi tasks Creates the tm-hotspot profile, or adopts an access-point profile made by hand, and ensures its device, priority, mode, address, and IPv6 setting. The password file is the source of truth for the password. It never activates or deactivates a profile, so a joined phone stays joined. Its docstring lists the order of its steps and its exit statuses. tm-network-retry tm-network-retry.timer, 90 seconds after boot and 5 minutes after each run ends, and the Hotspot check's Restart the hotspot Keeps the radio on a known network or on the hotspot. It starts the hotspot when no network holds the radio, leaves it alone while a phone is joined, and scans for the saved networks otherwise, one network per run, with a 5, 15, then 60 minute wait after each failure. Its docstring lists its steps and outcomes. It keeps its memory in /run/traffic-monitor/network-retry.json.

tm-hotspot-firewall.service loads the inet tm_hotspot nftables table before NetworkManager can start the hotspot. The table drops forwarded traffic into and out of the hotspot's subnet, so phones on it reach the unit and nothing behind it.

nginx's sign-in rule is in container/revproxy/nginx.conf.j2. On the hotspot dnsmasq answers every name with the unit's address, so a phone's connection test arrives with a foreign Host. A request that arrived on the hotspot's address with any name but that address or the unit's own is redirected to http://10.42.0.1/, which makes the phone open its sign-in window. The rule must never answer such a test with success: an Android 17 phone has no other way in. nginx also sets X-TM-Hotspot: 1 from the address a request arrived on, replacing any value the client sent, and GET /api/v1/setup/status then returns hotspot.local_name, which the login and setup pages show to an iPhone.

sudo tm-control card (core/card.py) prints the device's addresses, the hotspot's name and password, and the setup code. It refuses to run without root, reads the password and setup-code files and nmcli's answer first, and only then opens the state database. --json prints the same values, and --unclaimed-only, which the installer passes, prints nothing and exits 3 once the device is claimed.

docs.title: What the sandbox allows
docs.text:
tm-control.service runs with ProtectSystem=strict, RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_UNIX AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_NETLINK, and SupplementaryGroups=systemd-journal video. It writes its state and runtime directories and two config directories under the code directory (ReadWritePaths): Frigate's, frigate/config, for the models the Detection page manages, and Node-RED's, node-red-tm/config, for the config.yml the Location page writes. The rest of the system is read-only to it. The sandbox also shaped the probes:

  • The Coral USB check reads the vendor and product ids from /sys/bus/usb/devices rather than running lsusb, which needed a netlink socket the service first lacked, and ss falls back to reading /proc/net for the MQTT broker's port.
  • AF_NETLINK is there for iw, which reads the Wi-Fi country for the Network checks. The Network checks otherwise use nmcli, which needs nothing more, and never ask it for a password.
  • vcgencmd get_throttled needs the video group to open /dev/vcio_gencmd. Without it, the power check says to rerun the installer.
  • The HEVC decoder check compares /dev/rpi-hevc-dec with the media device whose /sys/bus/media/devices/mediaN/model names the decoder.
  • timedatectl show prints its times as local strings; tm-control reads the clock itself.
  • tm-control never writes the secrets directory; the set-secret job does.

docs.title: Run it on a laptop
docs.text:
Fake mode runs the whole app without a Pi: it uses the test manifest, fixed secrets that aren't secret, a job runner that pretends, a clock in memory for the Date and time page, a status report from tests/fixtures/status_fake.json, whose groups show every status and kind of fix, and a fake Node-RED for the Location page. Its state goes in ./.tm-control-fake/. From the repository root, in the dev environment from Contributing:

TM_CONTROL_FAKE=1 PYTHONPATH=tm-control/backend python -m tm_control fake-reset   # an unclaimed device; prints its setup code
TM_CONTROL_FAKE=1 PYTHONPATH=tm-control/backend python -m tm_control serve        # the backend on 127.0.0.1:8090
cd tm-control/ui && npm ci && npm run dev                                         # the UI on http://localhost:5173

Fake mode seeds .tm-control-fake/node-red-tm/config/config.yml from tests/fixtures/node_red_config_ok.yml (a camera and a radar, and a deployment block at 45.0, -122.0 with no survey id), and keeps it, with whatever the app wrote to it, until the next fake-reset. Its Node-RED (FakeNodeRed in fake.py) keeps deployment rows in memory and runs the deployment engine's rules on them whenever that file changes, so deploys, corrections, and hand edits of the file behave as on a device; after a restart of serve, only the place in use has deployments. Its backup directory is empty, so there's nothing to import. Fake mode also seeds .tm-control-fake/model_cache with two synthetic model pairs and the installer's model file, and keeps the model its fake Frigate runs in .tm-control-fake/running-model; Use there changes that file and restarts nothing. In fake mode the API's interactive docs are at /api/v1/docs. tm-control/ui/README.md has the commands for building and testing the UI in the same Node image the device uses.

Every change to the API regenerates the UI's typed client in the same commit, so each commit's tests pass:

PYTHONPATH=tm-control/backend python -m tm_control dump-openapi > tm-control/ui/src/api/openapi.json
(cd tm-control/ui && npm run api:generate)   # writes src/api/schema.d.ts

Run the backend's tests with the rest of the off-device tests:

.venv/bin/python -m pytest tm-control/backend/tests script/tests container/node-red-tm/schema/tests

docs.title: Add a module
docs.text:
A feature is one backend module and, if it has pages, one UI module.

  1. Backend: add backend/tm_control/modules/<name>/ with a router.py (an APIRouter) and an __init__.py that makes module = Module("<name>", router), with check_groups= if it has status checks. Add it to MODULES in modules/__init__.py. Endpoints take current_user or require_admin from modules/auth/deps.py, and raise ApiError for anything the operator should see.
  2. State: if it needs tables, add the next migration in core/state.py.
  3. UI: add ui/src/modules/<name>/ with its pages and an index.ts that lists its routes and menu entries, and add it to ui/src/modules/index.ts. Regenerate the typed client as the UI's README describes.
  4. Root work: prefer a polkit action or unit verb on the list. Otherwise add the job's name to JOB_NAMES in core/jobs.py, its script to tm-control/jobs/, its unit to the role's templates/tm-control/, and the unit to the polkit list.
  5. A new app behind the login: add its location file with an auth snippet to container/revproxy/tm/locations/ and to tmsetup_revproxy_locations, and its tile to APPS in modules/system/router.py and to ui/src/modules/home/apps.ts.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: A Traffic Monitor is a Raspberry Pi 5 running a few cooperating programs. Everything happens on the device, so it works without an internet connection once it's installed.

docs.title: From the street to the database
docs.text:
1. The camera streams H.265 video at 1536×864 and 10 frames per second to Frigate.
  2. Frigate finds and tracks objects in the video, using the AI accelerator if the device has one and the CPU if not. It records which zones each object passed through. When an object leaves the frame, Frigate publishes an event on the device's MQTT broker.
  3. The radar (optional) measures the speed and direction of whatever moves in front of it and reports readings over USB several times a second.

  4. Node-RED runs the Traffic Monitor logic. It keeps every radar reading, and it records every moving object from an enabled camera as an event. When the camera has a radar and the object entered any zone, it:

    • works out the direction of travel from the order in which the object entered zone_near and zone_far, or from the radar if the zones don't give one;
    • attaches a speed: the median radar reading in that direction while the object was in view, with a two-second margin on each side.

    Without a radar, events have no direction or speed. Direction and speed has the exact rules.

    The dashboards and the daily counts then filter the events by zone: they count objects that passed through zone_capture, and they use only objects that passed through zone_radar for speed statistics. 5. The database, one SQLite file on the device, stores the events, the radar readings, air quality readings from the optional sensor, and the device's deployment history. The dashboards read from it, and you can download it.

First-time setup walks through turning on detection and adjusting the four zones. Events lists every column an event has.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text: The device serves a home page at http://<device>/ that links to the dashboards, Frigate, and the system tools. Home page and apps describes each one.

docs.title: What stays on the device
docs.text: The database holds labels, times, speeds, and zones, not pictures. Frigate keeps cropped snapshots and short clips for about an hour so you can check what was detected, and nothing is sent anywhere unless you turn on an integration. Data and privacy has the details.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Three files on the device control the behavior described above. You edit them over SSH.

File What it controls Frigate's config.yml Camera, detection, zones, object filters, and recording. Most changes are made in Frigate's own web UI. See Tune object detection. Node-RED's config.yml Deployment location, which sensors are on, which radar pairs with which camera, and the ThingsBoard connection. Times shown on the dashboards use the device's time zone, which the installer sets and the control app's Date and time page changes. See config.yml settings. node-red-tm.env Radar serial ports, the database path, and the MQTT broker. See node-red-tm.env settings.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The dashboard shows no counts

Follow the checklist in First-time setup. The usual causes, in order: detection is off in Frigate, the objects don't pass through zone_capture, or the camera isn't enabled in config.yml.

Counts, but no speeds

The radar must be enabled in config.yml and named in the camera's camera_radar, zone_radar must cover the road, and the device must be at a shallow angle to the traffic. If the radar was plugged in after the software was installed, rerun bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm so the container can see it.

Frigate shows no camera image

Open Camera feeds from the home page, logged in as the administrator. If the picam_h265_detect stream plays there, the camera and its stream work, and the fault is between Frigate and the stream. Either the camera is off in Frigate's configuration editor, where cameras: picam_h265: needs enabled: true, or Frigate's video decoding is failing, which shows as ffmpeg errors in the frigate.service log. If the stream doesn't play, check the camera cable, then look at the go2rtc_server.service log in System administration.

Detection is slow or misses objects

Without an AI accelerator, Frigate detects on the CPU and can't keep up with a busy road. Hardware lists the supported accelerators. If you added one after installing, see Add an accelerator later. With an accelerator, see Tune object detection.

The home page opens on a computer but not on an Android phone

On Android 17, an app needs permission to reach devices on your local network. Browsers that don't have it time out on every device on the phone's own Wi-Fi network, including your router's page, while other apps and computers reach the device. Open the browser's app settings (Settings > Apps > Chrome, for example), allow Nearby devices or local network access if it's listed, force-stop the browser, and open the page again. If the browser has no such setting, use a computer or another phone. On the device's own hotspot, use the phone's sign-in window instead: Android 17 browsers can't open the device there. See Wi-Fi and the hotspot.

A hotspot I set up by hand doesn't show up on my phone

If you hid its name, the phone doesn't list it. On Android, choose Add network, type the name, and tick Hidden network. See A hotspot you set up by hand.

The first install seems stuck

Building Frigate's container image compiles ffmpeg on the device, which takes about 20 minutes with little output. Leave it running. The whole first install takes 30 minutes or more.

A database download fails

See Data export.

The Status page says the database schema is behind

Each time Node-RED starts, it updates the database's tables to the version the installed software expects. If an update fails, it's undone, and Node-RED runs on the old tables, where it may not be able to save new data. To see why it failed, run this over SSH or in Cockpit's terminal:

sudo journalctl -u node-red-tm | grep tmdb-migrate

If Node-RED started recently, the diagnostics on the Device page show the same lines. Restarting Node-RED tries the update again. If it fails again, ask for help and attach the diagnostics.

I edited config.yml and nothing changed

The Traffic Monitor reads the file again when you save it, so a change that doesn't take effect usually means a YAML error, such as a wrong indent or a missing space after a colon. The node-red-tm.service log in System administration shows the error. Fix the file before you restart the service; config.yml settings explains why.

docs.title: What does the device record?
docs.text: The database records what passed (a label such as car), when, how fast, and through which zones. It holds no images and no plate numbers with the default settings. Frigate keeps a cropped snapshot and a short clip of each detection for about an hour, so you can check what it saw, and you can turn that off. By default, the device sends no images or video anywhere: everything is processed on the device, and the database holds only metadata. The live view, the recordings, and Frigate's snapshots are behind the device's login, which decides who on your network can open the apps. It isn't a control on the images themselves: anyone with an account can see them, and they're ordinary files on the device's card. Data and privacy explains, and lists the features that would change what's stored.

docs.title: Why this design?
docs.text:
The Traffic Monitor is built privacy-first because we believe in:

  • Ethical and transparent monitoring. The code, the architecture, and the models are open, so anyone can see what the device does, and operators, especially public bodies, can be held to account.
  • Community safety and trust. Detection runs on the device, nothing is sent to an outside server unless you set it up, and the data stays in your control.
  • Unbiased data collection. Detection runs without human bias, but machine learning models can carry algorithmic bias. We use public-domain and open source models wherever possible and name the models in use.

To keep an area out of view, aim the camera so the area is out of frame. A motion mask doesn't hide it; see Data and privacy.

docs.title: How many objects can it track at once?
docs.text:
More than a busy street produces. The practical limit is objects hiding each other, as at the start of a race, where the camera can't see the person behind another.

The AI accelerator runs an inference in about 10 ms, which is about 100 inferences per second, and Frigate runs several inferences per frame when there's motion in several places. On a road with trees casting moving shadows, Frigate has been seen checking more than 18 motion regions and tracking 9 labeled objects at once, with inference time still around 9 ms. The video is decoded in hardware, and the CPU, which encodes the camera stream and runs motion detection, had headroom to spare. Frigate's discussions #7491 and #18326 explain how detections per frame are bounded.

A road where shadows produce many motion regions, all checked for objects

docs.title: Ideas and use cases
docs.text: The device collects more than counts. With extra zones in Frigate and the event data, you can study how people and vehicles interact. Two examples follow; share yours in Show and tell.

docs.title: Near misses at a crosswalk
docs.text:
A near miss is a driver and a vulnerable road user, such as a pedestrian at a crosswalk, in conflict at the same moment. These events are rarely captured today. The first step is a definition, and traffic law supplies one. As an example, Oregon's rules, summarized by Portland Bicycle School:

  • Every corner is a crosswalk (ORS 801.220).
  • A pedestrian has claimed the crossing as soon as any part of them, or their cane, wheelchair, or bicycle, enters it (ORS 811.028(4), 814.040(1)(a)).
  • A driver must stay stopped until the pedestrian has cleared the driver's lane, or the lane they're turning into, plus one more lane (ORS 811.028).

To capture conflicts:

  1. Mount the device with a view of the whole intersection.
  2. Draw zones for the pedestrian areas and the driver areas.
  3. Each person and car event then records its start_time, end_time, and entered_zones.
  4. Download the data and look for a car entering a driver zone while a person was in the conflicting pedestrian zone.

For example, a person in zone_ped_ne about to cross south or west, and a car that enters zone_intersection_e and turns into zone_intersection_n before the person has crossed, is a near miss or at least an illegal turn. You can tighten the definition further: was the car stationary at the stop sign first, or did a pedestrian zone at the very edge of the sidewalk show intent to cross? A person and a car in the same road zone at the same time is the most serious case.
