Zones for a near-miss study: pedestrian zones on each corner and intersection zones on each approach

docs.title: Vehicles that don't stop at a stop sign
docs.text:
A rolling stop, also called a California stop or Rhode Island stop, is a vehicle that passes a stop sign without stopping fully or for the required time. Some places let cyclists treat a stop sign as a yield (the Idaho stop).

  1. Mount the device high, looking down at the whole intersection.

  2. In Frigate, draw a thin stop-sign zone across the road just before each stop sign, such as zone_stop_sign_e and zone_stop_sign_w for a two-way stop.

  3. Give each stop-sign zone a loitering time that matches your jurisdiction, such as 3 seconds, and limit it to car if you like. The zone then appears in an event's entered_zones only if the vehicle stayed in it that long. A vehicle that rolled through has an event without the zone.

  4. Optionally add wider zones for each approach, so you can also see turning movements: a car that went from zone_intersection_e to zone_intersection_n turned right.

  5. Check the zones against a few real vehicles in Frigate's Explore view. It can take a while to find a car that stops properly.

docs.title: description: Where to ask questions, report bugs, and share ideas: the chat, GitHub discussions, and issues.
Get support
docs.text: The Traffic Monitor is a volunteer-run open source project. The community answers questions as it can, so please be patient, and help others when you can. Everyone follows the Code of Conduct.

docs.title: Search first
docs.text: Search these docs, then the repository: the search box at the top right covers discussions, issues, and code, with filters on the left.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text: The Traffic Monitor Zulip chat is the quickest place to ask a question, suggest an idea, or show a deployment. Developers discuss code there too, so it's also the place to start contributing.

docs.title: GitHub discussions
docs.text:
The discussions board is for longer conversations:

  • 💬 General: anything at all
  • 💡 Ideas: feature ideas, and votes on them
  • 🗳️ Polls
  • 🙏 Q&A: ask for help
  • 👐 Show and tell: what you've built

docs.title: GitHub issues
docs.text:
Open an issue for a specific bug, a feature request, or a technical question that the discussions haven't answered. Include enough detail for someone else to reproduce or understand it.

  • 🐞 Bug report
  • 💡 Feature request

An issue may be closed without a full resolution, for example as a duplicate, after inactivity, or because the work is tracked elsewhere. That isn't a lack of interest; comment or reopen if it still matters.

docs.title: Network ports
docs.text:
Other computers reach the Traffic Monitor's apps through the home page on port 80. The apps themselves, and the control app on port 8090, listen only on the device itself (loopback). The ports in the table below are the ones other computers can reach.

Port Used for 22 SSH 80 The control app and every app behind its login 1883 MQTT, only when the broker has a login. See MQTT and ThingsBoard. 5353 (UDP) <hostname>.local names (mDNS) 8554 The camera stream (RTSP), with a username and password 9090 Cockpit, with your Raspberry Pi login only. Use it if the home page doesn't load or the control app isn't answering.

docs.title: The hotspot
docs.text:
When the device's Wi-Fi isn't on a network it knows, it runs a hotspot on the built-in radio (wlan0).

Address The device is 10.42.0.1, on the network 10.42.0.0/24. The address is fixed. DHCP The device gives each phone an address in that network. DNS The device answers every name with its own address, so a phone's connection test lands on the device and opens the control app's sign-in window. Ports The same as on your network, in the table above. Reach A phone on the hotspot reaches only the device. A firewall rule drops anything that would pass from the hotspot to another network, or back, so the hotspot has no internet and doesn't open your wired network to a phone.

A request that reaches the device on the hotspot's address with any other name, such as the one a phone's connection test uses, gets a redirect to http://10.42.0.1/. A request for 10.42.0.1 or for the device's own name is answered as usual.

Whenever the device has a network, NetworkManager asks connectivity-check.ubuntu.com every 5 minutes whether the internet is reachable. The Status page's Internet check shows the answer.

docs.title: Camera stream login
docs.text:
The camera stream on port 8554 needs the username frigate and a password generated on the device at install. To play the stream in another program, such as VLC, read the password on the device:

sudo cat /etc/traffic-monitor/secrets/go2rtc_rtsp_password

Then open rtsp://frigate:<password>@<device>:8554/picam_h265_detect.

docs.title: Installer options
docs.text:
script/tmsetup.sh in the repository installs and updates the Traffic Monitor. Run it from the device, or from another computer with -H. Install the software and Update the software show the usual runs.

bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh [flags]

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Meaning -h Show the usage text and exit. -y Answer yes to every prompt, including the reboot. -v Verbose output. Repeat for more. -f Replace the user-editable settings files with fresh copies from the templates. See What -f replaces. -t TAG Run one component, plus anything that has to change with it. Repeat for several. See Tags. -T List the tags and exit. -C NAME[,NAME] Turn on an optional component: plate_recognizer (see Plate Recognizer), or mqtt_lan, which creates an MQTT broker login when there isn't one (see Connect from other devices). -u Also upgrade the operating system's packages (apt full-upgrade). -d PATH Install folder. Default /opt/traffic-monitor. The docs assume the default. -o USER Owner of the installed files and processes. Default tmadmin, created by the installer. -g GROUP Group of the installed files. Default tmadmin. -w CODE The Wi-Fi country, a two-letter code such as US or GB. Without it, the installer asks when the device has none and the run includes the wifi tag; with -y or a remote run it keeps the device's country, or sets US when there is none. See The Wi-Fi country. -z TIMEZONE Time zone for the system and the dashboards, as a tz database name. Default America/Los_Angeles. -L PATH Where to write the installer's log. -a ARG Pass an extra argument to the underlying Ansible run, without its leading hyphen.

Remote runs:

Flag Meaning -H HOST[,HOST] Install to these devices over SSH instead of the local machine. Separate several with commas. -l USER The SSH username on the devices. -k Ask for the SSH password. -K Ask for the password for administrator rights (sudo). Needed on Raspberry Pi OS unless you've set up passwordless sudo.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Each tag reruns one part of the install. Without -t, everything runs. The pod, the reverse proxy, and the control app that checks every login have to change together, so the podman, frigate, node-red-tm, go2rtc, revproxy, and tm-control tags each update all three.

Tag What it does base Operating system packages, the owner account, and Cockpit. It runs with every -t. full_upgrade The apt full-upgrade, when -u is given wifi The Wi-Fi country, the hotspot (its profile, its password file, the firewall that keeps phones on it from reaching other networks, and the DNS that sends every name on it to the device), and the timer that moves the radio between a saved network and the hotspot. It sets the hotspot's password to the one in the password file, and never restarts a hotspot that is up. go2rtc The camera streaming service on the host, and the stream login Frigate uses to read it detectors Detects the Coral or Hailo accelerator, installs its driver, and writes the boot configuration. See Add an accelerator later. podman The container runtime and the pod frigate Frigate's container, settings, and the devices it needs node-red-tm Node-RED's container, flows, settings, and the radars it needs. Rerun it after plugging in a radar. plate-recognizer The optional Plate Recognizer container revproxy The reverse proxy, with the home page built into its image tm-control The control app and its service, the tm-control command, the record of what was installed that the control app reads, and the setup code while the device isn't claimed. It also updates Frigate's config.yml from earlier versions: the stream login and the settings for the device's login.

docs.title: The device's card
docs.text: When a run on the device ends while the device is unclaimed, the installer shows its card on the terminal: the setup code, and the hotspot's name and password. The card goes only to the terminal, so the hotspot's password stays out of the installer's log; the setup code is still in it. A run from another computer with -H prints a reminder only. sudo tm-control card prints the card on the device at any time.

docs.title: What -f replaces
docs.text:
Every run replaces the container images, service units, Node-RED flows, and the reverse proxy configuration. These files are kept unless you pass -f:

  • /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml
  • /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/node-red-tm.env
  • /opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/config/config.yml, which holds zones and masks drawn in Frigate
  • /opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/frigate.env. Its Frigate+ key comes from the device's secrets.
  • /opt/traffic-monitor/plate-recognizer/plate-recognizer.env, if Plate Recognizer is installed. Its token and license key come from the device's secrets.

With -f, each is replaced by a fresh copy from its template, and the old file stays next to it with a timestamp in its name so you can copy your settings back. The MQTT broker login carries into the fresh node-red-tm.env and frigate.env. A fresh Frigate config has detection off and the sample zones, so afterwards turn detection on and redo your zones and masks, as in First-time setup.

The fresh Frigate config keeps one thing from the old one: the model: section, if you chose a model, whether in Frigate's model picker, its configuration editor, or by hand (see Better models). It's kept even when Frigate can't load that model; see If Frigate stops over a model. The installer's own model section for a Coral isn't kept, so the fresh copy gets the model for the accelerator the installer finds. Comments inside a kept section are lost; its keys keep their order. If the old config isn't valid YAML, the fresh copy gets the installer's model section, and the installer says so.

No run, with or without -f, replaces the device's accounts, its setup code, or the passwords and keys in /etc/traffic-monitor/secrets/, including the ThingsBoard token, the Frigate+ API key, and the Plate Recognizer token and license key you entered. The installer writes those values into node-red-tm.env, frigate.env, and plate-recognizer.env on every run, so a fresh copy from -f has them too. The installer takes no secret value as an option: enter them on the Device page, or the Frigate+ key on the Detection page.

docs.title: Add an accelerator later
docs.text:
After you add or change a Coral or Hailo accelerator, rerun two tags and reboot when the installer asks:

bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t detectors -t frigate

That installs the driver and gives Frigate's container the device. Frigate's own config.yml still names the old detector, because the installer writes its detectors: and model: sections only when it creates the file. Either edit those two sections by hand to match the template, or add -f to the command above and then redo your Frigate settings, as What -f replaces describes.

-f keeps a model you chose, such as a Frigate+ model, and that model may not suit the new accelerator. If it doesn't, Frigate can't use it and counts nothing, and the Status page reports the problem. Pick a model built for the new accelerator (see Use a model), or, to get the installer's model for it, delete the model: section in Frigate's configuration editor before you run the installer with -f.

docs.title: Reboots
docs.text: The installer edits the boot configuration and installs kernel drivers, so it asks to reboot when needed. On the device, it prompts, and with -y it doesn't ask. Either way the reboot starts one minute later. Remote devices reboot by themselves. Services stay stopped until the reboot.

docs.title: description: The Data export dashboard: download the database or a JSON export, and add comments for whoever analyzes the data.
Data export
docs.text:
Open http://<device>/dashboard/database, or Database in the dashboard's sidebar. This page gets data off the device and lets you leave notes in it. Both downloads need the device's administrator login; a viewer can open the page but not download.

The Data export page

docs.title: Comments
docs.text: A comment is a timestamped note stored in the comments table, for whoever analyzes the data later: a settings change, road work, an event in the area. Give it an effective date and an optional expiry date, the text, and your name; only the name is required. The form also has time fields, but only the dates are kept. Without an effective date, the comment takes effect when you save it. Data and privacy lists the columns.

docs.title: Download the database
docs.text:
Downloads the whole database as a compressed archive named <hostname>_<time>_tmdb.tar.gz. The page shows the database's size in megabytes. The device first makes a consistent copy of the database, so a large one can take a minute or two before the download starts. The copy needs free space about the size of the database; if there isn't enough, the page says so. A 3 GB file can then take about 5 minutes to compress and several more to download. Cancel also works while the copy is being made: the download stops once the copy is done, and no archive is sent. If a download fails, you see the reason instead of a broken file.

On a phone joined to the unit's hotspot, see Phones for how downloads save on Android and on an iPhone.

Unpack the archive with tar -xvzf on Linux or Mac, or with 7-Zip on Windows. Inside is tmdb.sqlite, which opens in DB Browser for SQLite or any SQLite library.

docs.title: Download JSON
docs.text:
Exports part of the data as JSON files in a compressed archive named <hostname>_<time>_json.tar.gz. Choose what to export and a start and end time, which default to the last 7 days:

Choice Contents Everything The events table, the five radar tables, and the airquality table All event types The whole events table for the time range One object type, such as car or person The events of that type Air quality The airquality table Radar The radar tables

The files are plain JSON, readable in any text editor or loaded straight into a notebook.

docs.title: description: The Monitoring dashboard: today's counts, car speed statistics, hourly and daily charts, and the latest events with their radar readings.
Monitoring
docs.text:
Open http://<device>/dashboard/monitoring, or open Dashboard from the home page and choose Monitoring in the sidebar. Monitoring shows the counts and speed statistics for one camera and one radar at a time.

The Monitoring page, numbered as in the list below
  1. Sensor selection. A radar and a camera picker, listing every sensor in config.yml, enabled or not. The counts and statistics on this page follow the camera and radar selected on the legacy dashboard at http://<device>/ui/, not the selection here. On a device with one camera and one radar, they're the same.

  2. Car speed statistics for the current day, which starts at 04:00 local time. They cover car events that passed through both zone_capture and zone_radar and got a speed from the radar. Speeds are absolute values, so inbound and outbound are pooled, and every value is rounded to a whole number.

    The percentiles come from sorting the day's cars by speed and splitting them into 20 groups of equal size, so they're approximate. With few cars, some stay empty: the 25th percentile needs 5 cars, the median 10, the 75th percentile and iqr_upper 15, and the 85th percentile 17.

    Statistic Meaning count Cars with a speed mean_speed Average speed p25_speed, p50_speed, p75_speed, p85_speed 25th, 50th (median), 75th, and 85th percentile speeds. The 85th percentile is the usual basis for speed limits. max_speed Fastest car count_over_25 Cars faster than 25, in the radar's units iqr_upper The outlier line: p75_speed plus 1.5 times the interquartile range iqr_upper_freq Cars faster than iqr_upper, the outliers

  3. Today's counts by object type for events that passed through zone_capture. The day starts at 04:00 local time, so from midnight until 04:00 these counts and the speed statistics are empty. Objects that pass in those hours are left out of the day's counts, but they appear in the hourly and daily charts.

  4. Hourly counts by object type for the last 36 hours, for events that passed through zone_capture.
  5. Daily counts by object type for the last 10 calendar days, for events that passed through zone_capture.
  6. Latest observations. The 21 most recent events from any camera that passed through zone_radar, newest first, including events without a speed. Each card shows Frigate's thumbnail of the object, the direction, the speed, and the radar's raw readings from the start of the event to its end: how many there were ("radar hits"), the range of their magnitudes and speeds, and two charts, Radar Magnitude and Radar Speed. The charts show whether the readings came from one object or from several at once. They're the raw readings, not the ones the speed was worked out from. The list is kept in memory, so it empties when Node-RED restarts.

Counts and statistics come from the events table; see Events. The same counts are published over MQTT on tm/events; see MQTT and ThingsBoard.

docs.title: description: The Movements dashboard: counts of objects by the sequence of zones they passed through, for checking against manual counts.
Movements
docs.text:
Open http://<device>/dashboard/movements. Movements counts objects by the path they took through your zones, which is how you check the device against a manual count or confirm that the zones capture what you want.

Movements come from the entered_zones of each event, so they depend on how the zones are drawn.

The Movements page
  1. Zones. Tick the zones to include. The four standard zone_* zones are unticked by default, so that zones you drew for your own analysis stand out.
  2. Intermediate zones. Choose Show intermediate zones to count each full sequence of zones separately, or Show just initial & final zones to group by where an object entered and where it left.
  3. Time range. Start and end times; the last 7 days by default. In time zones east of UTC, or with a half-hour offset, the page shows no counts for any range.
  4. Counts by object type for each zone sequence that matches.

docs.title: Example: a complex intersection
docs.text:
An intersection with many zones has dozens of possible movements. Each turn or crossing becomes its own row, which you can compare with a manual count sheet.

Twelve zones drawn on a busy five-way intersection Manual confirmation counts; the left sheet matches the zones above

docs.title: Control app and login
docs.text:
The device's home page is its control app. It holds the device's accounts, and one login there opens the apps your account may use: the dashboards, Frigate, the Node-RED editor, the camera feeds, and Cockpit. Its Status, Device, and Date and time pages show whether the device works and help you fix it; see Check and fix the device. Its Detection page shows the object detection model and lets the administrator change it; see Choose the detection model. Its Location page records where the device is and how precisely the database stores it; see Places and location. These accounts belong to the device. They're separate from the Raspberry Pi user account you created when you imaged the card. That account's password is the system password.

What the login protects

The login keeps people on your network out of the apps. The device uses plain HTTP, so passwords and images cross your network unencrypted. Use the device on a network you trust.

docs.title: Claim the device
docs.text:
A device that has no administrator yet sends every page to setup. That happens on a new device, after an update from a version without the login, and after reset-admin. Setup has four steps: a welcome page, the license agreement, the administrator account, and the system password.

You need the setup code, eight letters and digits written as XXXX-XXXX. It comes from one of two places:

  • A pre-built unit: the card that came with the device.

  • A device you installed yourself: the end of the installer's output, in a line like this one:

    This device isn't claimed yet. Open http://tm-01.local/ (or its IP address) and enter the setup code ABCD-EFGH
to create the administrator account. The code works once.

    The installer prints the same code on every run until the device is claimed. The installer's log, ~/tmsetup-<date>-<time>.log on the computer that ran it, has the same output. On the device, sudo tm-control card shows the code with the device's hotspot name and password, and sudo cat /etc/traffic-monitor/setup-code shows the code alone.

To claim the device:

  1. Open http://<device>/. Home page and apps explains how to find the address. On the device's own hotspot, the phone's sign-in window opens it for you; see Wi-Fi and the hotspot.
  2. Choose Start setup, read the license agreement, and accept it.
  3. Enter the setup code, then a username and password for the administrator account. Usernames are 3 to 32 characters: lowercase letters, digits, dots, dashes, and underscores. Passwords are at least 10 characters.
  4. Choose Claim this device. You're logged in as the administrator.
  5. Set a new system password, or choose Skip for now.
Step 3 of setup creates the administrator account

The code works once. After several wrong codes, setup makes you wait before the next try, a little longer after each wrong code.

When the license agreement changes

An update can bring a new version of the license agreement. Until the administrator accepts it, nobody can open the apps. The administrator sees the new version after logging in. Viewers see Waiting for an administrator until it's accepted.

docs.title: The system password
docs.text: The system password is the password of the Raspberry Pi user account: the one you log in to Cockpit and SSH with. Setup offers to change it, with a Use the same password as my account checkbox. Skip the step to keep the password the account has. To change it later, use Cockpit's Accounts page, or run passwd over SSH.

docs.title: Log in
docs.text:
Open the home page or any app. Without a session, the device shows its login page, then takes you to the page you asked for. You stay logged in for a week, and using the device keeps the session going. To log out, choose Log out in the menu. Frigate's own Logout also logs you out of the device.

After five wrong passwords in a row, the device makes you wait before the next try: a few seconds at first, and twice as long after each further wrong password, up to 5 minutes. It counts wrong passwords for the account and for the address they come from, so a wait for an account applies on every phone and computer. Sessions that are already logged in keep working. The count clears 15 minutes after the last wrong password, or when the login succeeds.

docs.title: Administrators and viewers
docs.text:
Each device has one administrator, the account created when it was claimed, and any number of viewers.

App or page Administrator Viewer Dashboard and Legacy Dashboard Yes Yes Downloads on the Data export page Yes No Frigate: live view, review, and explore Yes Yes Frigate: settings and the configuration editor Yes No Node-RED editor, Camera feeds, and Cockpit Yes No The Users page Yes No Status, Device, and Date and time pages Yes Read only; see What viewers see The Detection page Yes Read only; see The Detection page The Location page Yes No

docs.title: Add a viewer
docs.text:
1. Open Users from the menu.
  2. Under Add a viewer, enter a username and a password, and choose Add viewer.
  3. Give the person the username and password.

Each viewer's menu on the Users page has Set a new password, which also logs them out everywhere, and Remove.

docs.title: Change your password
docs.text:
Open Account from the menu. Under Change your password, enter your current password and the new one. Every other browser and phone where you were logged in is logged out; this one stays logged in. Wrong current passwords count toward the same wait as wrong logins.

Log out everywhere, on the same page, ends your sessions in every browser and on every phone, including the one you're using. Use it if you logged in on a device that isn't yours.

docs.title: If you forget a password
docs.text:
• A viewer's password: the administrator sets a new one on the Users page.
  • The administrator's password: see the next section.

docs.title: If the administrator's password is lost
docs.text:
Someone who can log in to the device with the Raspberry Pi user account can start over. Open a terminal over SSH, or in Cockpit at http://<device>:9090, and run:

sudo tm-control reset-admin

It removes every account, the administrator and all viewers, and prints a new setup code. Then claim the device again with that code. Your data and settings stay as they are.

docs.title: If the control app is down
docs.text:
When the control app doesn't answer, the apps can't check your login. Every app then shows a page that says the control app isn't answering, and the home page says The control app isn't answering. To start it again:

  • In a browser, open Cockpit at http://<device>:9090. It doesn't need the control app. Log in with your Raspberry Pi user account, go to Services, open tm-control.service, and restart it.

  • Over SSH, run:

    sudo systemctl restart tm-control.service
sudo journalctl -u tm-control.service -n 50   # if it stops again, the reason is in its log

An app that's down while the control app works, such as Frigate during a restart, shows a 502 Bad Gateway error instead. System administration covers the services and their logs.

docs.title: Choose the detection model
docs.text: The control app's Detection page shows what the device looks for and which AI model does the looking, and lets the administrator change the model without SSH. Frigate runs the model on the device's detector: a Coral or Hailo accelerator, or the processor when there's none. To get a better model for a difficult site, see Better models.

docs.title: The Detection page
docs.text:
Detection is in the control app's menu, after Device. The page opens with a line on what it's for, then four sections:

  • Object detection gives the Detector, such as edgetpu for a Coral, and the Running model, then what the running model recognises and what the device tracks.
  • Model in use is the model Frigate runs. The section is left out when the page can't tell which model that is.
  • Other models on this device lists the rest, and its title counts them.
  • Frigate+ is how to get a Frigate+ model, and where administrators set the API key.

Each model is a card with its name, its kind (Frigate+ or local), and when it was trained and what it's built for (when it says). Select Files and objects on a card to see its files, with their sizes and the start of each file's SHA-256 hash, and the objects it recognises. A model with no list of objects has Files instead. A mark says when the model is:

Mark Meaning In use Frigate runs this model. can't run on this detector The model is built for another detector than the device's, so Use is off. incomplete The model has its file but not its .json, or the other way round.

The model the installer set up is shown as The installer's model. It has no .json, and it can't be deleted. A device without a Coral has no installer's model: Frigate then runs its own built-in model until you choose another, and the page shows it as Frigate's built-in model, which can't be deleted either.

Everyone who can log in sees the models, the label lists, and the Frigate+ text. Administrators also get Upload a model, under the Other models on this device heading, then Use, Download, and Delete on each model, and the Frigate+ API key. While Frigate runs another model, the device's default (the installer's model, or Frigate's built-in model on a device without a Coral) has a Use of its own.

When Frigate isn't answering, the page says so and shows what Frigate's config file says. The same when Frigate started in safe mode because it couldn't use its config: the page says so, nothing is detected meanwhile, and Use on a model, or on the installer's model, gives Frigate a config it can run.

docs.title: Upload a model
docs.text:
A model is a model file and a small .json file beside it, its sidecar, which tells Frigate how to use it. Choose Upload a model under Other models on this device, then pick one of these:

  • A package from whoever trained the model: a zip or tar.gz with the model file and its .json at the top level, not inside a folder. A zip must be stored or deflate-compressed, which is what ordinary zip tools make. If the package has a SHA256SUMS file, the device checks the files against it.
  • The two files, the model file and its .json. The .json must be named for the model file: mine.tflite and mine.tflite.json. The page sends the .json first.
  • A model file alone. The page then asks for what Frigate needs to know about it and writes the .json for you. The settings are a name for the model list (the file name when left empty), the model type, the width and height of its input, the input tensor, the pixel format, optionally the input data type, and the labels, one per line in the model's order. On a device with a Coral or Hailo accelerator, the fields start with Frigate's example for that detector. The values come from the model's documentation; Frigate's reference config lists what each setting accepts.
  • A .json alone, to finish a model file that's on the device already.

The page shows every file when you pick, because a Frigate+ model's file has no extension.

The limits are 100 MB for a model file, 2 MB for a .json, and at least 512 MB of free storage left afterwards. A model whose name is already on the device is refused; delete the old one first. A model file can't be named default, which the page keeps for the device's default. A model has to be built for the device's detector. The page marks one that isn't, and won't use it.

Take models only from a source you trust

A model is code that the detector runs. A model from an unknown source can make the device count wrongly or fail. Upload only models you trained, or that come from a source you trust.

docs.title: Use a model
docs.text:
Choose Use on a model and confirm. Frigate checks the whole configuration with the model in it and saves it, and then the device restarts Frigate. A restart takes about a minute, and the device counts nothing meanwhile. The page asks every few seconds and says when Frigate runs the model. If Frigate hasn't come back after 90 seconds, the page says so and links to the Status page.

If Frigate refuses the change, the page shows Frigate's reason, and nothing changes. When Frigate isn't answering at all, the device edits Frigate's config.yml itself, keeps a backup beside it, and restarts Frigate. That's how Use on The installer's model gets a device out of a bad choice without SSH. On a device without a Coral, Use on Frigate's built-in model does the same.

The page refuses a Use in these cases:

  • Frigate is restarting. Try again in a minute.
  • The device's detector can't be told, because Frigate isn't answering and its config file can't be read, so the model can't be checked against it.
  • Frigate's config sets a model inside a detector, which would override this one. Remove that model in Frigate's config editor first.
  • The installer's model file is gone from the device.

docs.title: Download a model
docs.text:
Download saves a zip with the model's file, its .json, and a SHA256SUMS file. The files are byte for byte what's on the device, so the zip is a backup, or a way to put the same model on another device with Upload a model. A .json keeps every field it came with, including ones the page doesn't show.

A model without a .json the device can read downloads as its model file alone, under the file's own name, and the page says so before it starts. Whoever uploads that file is asked for what Frigate needs to know about it. The installer's model and Frigate's built-in model download this way too. A device keeps their file names for its own copies, so rename such a file before you upload it.

docs.title: Delete a model
docs.text: Delete asks first, then removes both of the model's files. It can't remove the model Frigate runs, the installer's model, or Frigate's built-in model. To delete the model that's running, use another model first, such as The installer's model.

docs.title: What the model recognises
docs.text:
The Object detection section lists two sets of objects. Each is closed until you select its title, which counts the objects, and each has a Copy button:

  • Objects the running model recognises is what the running model can detect. The list says where it came from: Frigate when it answers, otherwise the model's .json or the installer's labels file. Objects the device also tracks are filled. Frigate fills the gaps in a model's label map with entries named unknown, which the page leaves out, so its count can be lower than the label map's.
  • Objects tracked on this device is the objects Frigate is set to track, from its objects: track lists. Objects the running model doesn't recognise are amber, and the title counts them.

Frigate tracks only the objects in both lists. To track more of what the model recognises, change the lists in Frigate's configuration editor; see Tune object detection. An object that's tracked but not recognised is also named under the two lists, so you see it while they're closed. The model can't detect it, so the device never counts it.

Each model's card has its own list under Files and objects, read from that model's .json or, for the installer's model, its labels file. Frigate's built-in model has none. On the other models' cards, a line names the tracked objects that model doesn't recognise, which the device would stop counting if you switched to it.

The running model's list and its card are read in different ways, but they should agree. When Frigate's list has different objects, a line under the facts says "Frigate reports a different list than this model's .json." This is rare, and it usually means someone edited the label map in Frigate's config on purpose.

docs.title: Frigate+
docs.text:
Frigate+ trains models on snapshots from your device. There are two ways to get one onto it:

  • Online: when the device has internet and a Frigate+ API key, pick the model in Frigate, under Settings > System > Detectors and model, and Frigate downloads it. Then choose Use here if Frigate doesn't run it already.
  • Offline: upload the model's two files on this page, as a package from whoever trained the model, or copied from another device's Frigate. See A device without internet.

Administrators enter the API key under Frigate+, the last section of the page, which is closed until you select its title. The Status page's Set the key opens it. The key is kept with the device's other secrets, not in config.yml.

  • The page never shows the key back. The section's title says whether the key is set, its last four characters for a key of 12 or more characters, and "in use" while Frigate runs a Frigate+ model.
  • Save stores what you typed. A key is 36 characters, a colon, and 40 lowercase letters or digits, as Frigate+ shows it; the page refuses anything else. The eye icon shows the key while you type.
  • Remove asks first, then empties the key. Without a key, snapshots can't be submitted to Frigate+. A Frigate+ model whose files are on the device keeps running; one that isn't downloaded yet stops Frigate until the key is set again, and the Status page's Frigate+ check says so.
  • Saving or removing restarts Frigate, which takes about a minute. The device counts nothing meanwhile.

The ThingsBoard and Plate Recognizer keys are on the Device page.

docs.title: Check and fix the device
docs.text:
Three pages in the control app's menu tell you whether the device works and let the administrator fix the common problems from a phone, without SSH. A fourth, Detection, shows the object detection model and changes it:

  • Status checks the services, apps, settings, hardware, network, and clock, and offers a fix for what's wrong.
  • Device shows the device's facts and software versions, and has the diagnostics download, reboot, and shut down.
  • Date and time compares the device's clock with your phone's or computer's and sets it.

The home page shows the Status page's summary under the device's name, such as Everything is working. Tap it to open the Status page.

docs.title: The Status page
docs.text:
The page opens with one sentence about the whole device:

Summary Meaning Everything is working Every check passed. Working, with 2 things to look at Some checks have a warning, and none has a problem. 2 problems need attention At least one check has a problem. Some checks couldn't run Some checks couldn't get an answer, and none found a warning or a problem.

Below it, each check shows a mark, its name, and one or two sentences about what it found and what to do. A tick means it passed, a triangle a warning, a cross a problem, and a question mark that the check couldn't run. The page checks again every 10 seconds while it's open. Refresh checks at once.

The checks come in groups:

Group What it checks Services Each Traffic Monitor service: running, stopped, starting, or running after restarts that followed failures. Frigate restarts itself when you save its config; that doesn't count as a failure. When it restarts itself again and again within minutes, as when its AI accelerator has failed, that does count, and the row says so. Apps Frigate answers, isn't in safe mode (with no cameras because of a config error), and gets frames from each camera. When Frigate stopped on an error, the Frigate check quotes it. When Frigate isn't answering because it keeps stopping itself, the check says so and points at the Hardware group and the diagnostics. Node-RED answers, loaded config.yml without errors, and has its database at the version this install expects. The camera streams run, and Frigate reads them. The MQTT broker requires its login while port 1883 is open to the network. Configuration Frigate and config.yml agree on the names that link them: each Frigate camera is enabled in config.yml, it has the zones zone_capture, zone_near, zone_far, and zone_radar, each radar under sensors.radars is named after one of the TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_ variables in node-red-tm.env, and each camera's radar is enabled. The Location check is a problem when a deployment value in config.yml is one Node-RED won't accept, such as a coordinate out of range or a bearing with spaces around it, and names the key. It warns when a sensor still has its own lat or lon, when the device's places haven't been set up since an update, which the control app does by itself once Node-RED answers, and when survey_id names a place the device doesn't have, and links to the Location page. In safe mode Frigate has no cameras, so the checks that read them, here and in the Apps group, report that they couldn't run and point at the Frigate check. It also checks the ThingsBoard upload: its settings, and that a token is set when the upload is on. The Frigate+ check says whether a Frigate+ key and a Frigate+ model are set together, and whether Frigate can use the model; see The Frigate+ check. See config.yml settings and First-time setup. Hardware Each AI accelerator, from plugged in to passed to Frigate and listed in its config, or a warning when there's none and Frigate detects on the CPU. Whether detection works is Frigate's to report: when its detector keeps failing, Frigate restarts itself, and the Services and Apps rows say so. The video decoder Frigate uses for the camera. Each radar, from plugged in to read by Node-RED. Network The device's Wi-Fi, in four checks. An offline device is normal, so none of them is a problem for lack of internet. See The Network group. Device Free storage (a warning under 2 GB, a problem under 512 MB), free memory (a warning under 200 MB), the processor's temperature (a warning from 80 °C, a problem from 85 °C), and the power supply: whether the Pi ran short of power or slowed itself down since it started. Date and time Whether the clock was ever set, and whether it keeps time from the internet.

docs.title: The Network group
docs.text:
Check What it says Hotspot On as TM-4F2A, at http://10.42.0.1/ while the hotspot is up. Standing by while the device is on a saved network; the hotspot starts when that network is out of reach. Off by choice when the hotspot is turned off. A problem when the hotspot isn't set up (rerun the installer with -t wifi), the Wi-Fi radio is switched off, the hotspot should be on and isn't (Restart the hotspot), the hotspot has no password (see A hotspot you set up by hand), a USB Wi-Fi adapter has taken the built-in radio's place, or the hotspot's firewall isn't loaded. A warning when the hotspot isn't secured with WPA2. Wi-Fi network The network the device is on and its signal, or that it has no saved network, or that none of the saved networks is in reach. Internet Reachable, or Not reachable. That's normal for an offline unit. It also says when the network needs a sign-in page, so the device has no internet. It is never a warning or a problem. Wi-Fi country The country, or a warning that none is set. Rerun the installer with -t wifi and it asks; see The Wi-Fi country.

A check that can't read the Wi-Fi state shows a question mark.

docs.title: Fix a problem
docs.text:
A check that isn't passing offers one of these:

  • A Restart button, such as Restart Frigate, for a service that stopped or keeps failing. The Hotspot check's Restart the hotspot has the device look at its Wi-Fi radio and start the hotspot if it should be on. The device asks first and says what you'll notice, for example that traffic isn't counted while Frigate restarts. A note under the button says when the restart is under way.
  • Re-scan hardware, at the end of the Hardware group while one of its checks isn't passing. It runs every check again at once, so you don't wait for the next check after you plug a device back in or follow the check's advice.
  • A link to the page that fixes it, such as Set the date and time, Diagnostics on the Device page, or Set the token for the ThingsBoard upload, which opens Tokens and keys, or Set the key for Frigate+, which opens the Frigate+ API key section of the Detection page, or Open the Location page for the Location check.
  • A sentence with the next step, such as rerunning the installer for Node-RED (tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm; see Installer options).

The control app can't restart itself. If it stops, see If the control app is down.

docs.title: The Device page
docs.text: The card at the top shows the device's name, its Raspberry Pi model and memory, the Traffic Monitor version, the serial number, how long it has been running, its free storage, the processor's temperature, and the power supply's state. Software lists the versions of Frigate, Node-RED, go2rtc, nginx, and the Hailo driver if installed, the Traffic Monitor commit, the operating system, and the kernel.

docs.title: Tokens and keys
docs.text:
Administrators set the credentials the device uses for outside services in Tokens and keys. The section is closed when the page opens; select its heading to open it. The Status page's Set the token link opens it for you. It lists the ThingsBoard access token, and the Plate Recognizer API token and license key when the Plate Recognizer add-on is installed. Each is kept with the device's other secrets, not in config.yml. The Frigate+ API key is on the Detection page, next to the models it fetches.

  • A value is never shown back. The page says whether it's set and, for a token or key of 12 or more characters, its last four characters, so you can tell which one you entered. It never shows any of the license key.
  • Save stores what you typed in the box. The eye icon shows it while you type. A ThingsBoard token takes letters, digits, and . _ ~ -. A Plate Recognizer value takes printable ASCII characters without spaces. Both are up to 256 characters long.
  • Remove asks first, then empties the value. Without a ThingsBoard token the upload stops, and without the Plate Recognizer values plates aren't read.
  • Saving or removing restarts the app that uses the value, and the page waits for it. The ThingsBoard token and the license key restart one app and take about thirty seconds. The Plate Recognizer API token restarts the add-on and Node-RED, which takes about a minute. Traffic isn't counted while Node-RED restarts.

An older device may have kept a token in config.yml or in the add-on's env file, or a Frigate+ key in frigate.env. The installer moves it to the device's secrets, so uploads, plate reads, and Frigate+ keep working, and the Device page and the Detection page show it as set. A warning on the Status page's ThingsBoard upload check says when config.yml still holds a token key, which nothing reads, or when the upload is on without a token.

docs.title: Download diagnostics
docs.text:
When you ask for help, send the diagnostics with your question. It's a text file with the device's facts, its date and time settings, every status check, the services' states, what the installer installed and found, and the last 50 lines of each service's log. Passwords, keys, tokens, and the setup code are replaced with <redacted>. The file names the device and holds its serial number.

  • Download diagnostics saves the file.
  • Copy puts the text on the clipboard, ready to paste into a message. If the browser doesn't allow it, the page shows the text in a box, already selected, for you to copy.

docs.title: Reboot or shut down
docs.text:
Reboot the device and Shut down the device each ask before they act. A reboot takes about two minutes, during which no page answers. If something such as a system update is holding the device up, or the control app isn't allowed to, the device says it can't reboot or shut down right now. Try again in a few minutes, and if it keeps happening, download the diagnostics.

Shut down only when you can reach the device

After a shutdown, nothing starts the device again from the network. To turn it back on, unplug its power and plug it back in.

docs.title: The Date and time page
docs.text:
The page shows two clocks side by side: This device and This browser (the phone or computer you're using), each with its date and offset from UTC. Under them, a sentence says whether they agree, or how far apart they are and whether their time zones differ.

  • Set from this browser sends your browser's time and time zone to the device. If the device already has its time from the internet, it keeps that time, and only the time zone changes. Otherwise it takes your browser's time. If the device doesn't know your browser's time zone, which can happen when your phone or computer has a newer list of zones, it still takes the time, leaves its time zone as it was, and asks you to pick one from the list.
  • Time zone: pick a zone, type part of its name to find it, then choose Save time zone. The installer sets the first time zone (its -z option, see Installer options); this page changes it later. The dashboards show times, and start each day at 04:00, in the device's time zone.
  • Keep time from the internet turns internet time on or off. The sentence under the switch says where the device's time comes from now.

Changing the time zone restarts Frigate, Node-RED, and the web proxy, so they all use the new zone. The page stops answering for a moment, and traffic isn't counted for about a minute.

Moving the clock ahead by more than about 20 seconds stops Frigate's camera feed, and a move of a few minutes can stop it until Frigate restarts. So when a change moves the clock ahead by that much, the device restarts Frigate and the page says so. Traffic isn't counted for about a minute. Moving the clock back restarts nothing, unless internet time briefly puts the device's later time back while it's being set, and then the page says so.

When the device has no internet

A Raspberry Pi keeps no time while it's off, unless it has a clock battery. A device without internet then starts with a clock that may be wrong. The Status page's Clock check shows a warning that no time source is reachable, or a problem if the date is before 2026. Open Date and time on your phone or computer and choose Set from this browser. The clock is usually behind after a power-off, so this moves it ahead and restarts Frigate; the camera is back in about a minute. Internet time stays on, so the device corrects its clock by itself once it's online; until then the warning stays. If the device's clock was ahead, turning internet time back on puts that wrong time back, so the device sets your time again, leaves internet time off, and the page says so. Turn on Keep time from the internet once the device is online. If that puts the wrong time back for a moment, the device restarts Frigate; the camera is back in about a minute. If a later correction stops the camera, the Status page offers Restart Frigate. A device that is never online keeps time from its own clock, which drifts; set it again now and then.

docs.title: What viewers see
docs.text:
Viewers see all four pages, but can't change anything:

  • Status: the same checks, without the Restart and Re-scan buttons.
  • Device: the card and the software versions, without Tokens and keys, Diagnostics, and Power.
  • Detection: the models and the label lists, without the action buttons and the Frigate+ key form; see Choose the detection model.
  • Date and time: the clocks, the time zone, and where the time comes from, without the button, the zone picker, or the switch.

docs.title: description: The device's home page and the apps it links to: dashboards, Frigate, Node-RED, camera feeds, and Cockpit.
Home page and apps
docs.text:
Open http://<device>/ in a browser on the same network. <device> is the hostname you set when you imaged the card, followed by .local (for example http://tm-01.local/), or the device's IP address.

The home page is the device's control app. A new device first asks you to claim it with its setup code; after that, the home page and every app ask you to log in. The home page shows the device's name, software version, serial number, and time, a one-line summary of its health, and links to the apps your account can open. Its menu has Status, Device, and Date and time (see Check and fix the device), Detection (see Choose the detection model), Location for administrators (see Places and location), your Account, the Users page for administrators, and Log out.

Link Path What it is Who can open it Dashboard /dashboard/ The Traffic Monitor dashboards: Monitoring, Movements, and Data export, which opens first. Switch pages in the sidebar. Any user. The Data export downloads need an administrator. Frigate /frigate/ Object detection: live view, detections with snapshots and clips, zones, masks, and the Frigate settings. See Tune object detection. Any user. Frigate's settings need an administrator. Legacy Dashboard /ui/ The older dashboard, with the same counts and speed statistics as Monitoring. It's the only dashboard that shows air quality readings, and the Monitoring dashboard's counts follow its camera and radar selection. Its System Settings tab shows the device's name, time zone, and software versions, and holds the ThingsBoard Backup & Restore section. Any user Node-RED editor /nr/ The flow editor, for developers. See Dev environment. Administrators Camera feeds /feeds/ The camera streams the Pi camera produces, for checking that the camera works. It's for watching only: go2rtc's settings, stream editor, and log pages aren't available here. Administrators Cockpit /system/ Services, logs, containers, and a terminal. See System administration. Administrators, who then log in with the Raspberry Pi user account Finding the device's address
  • If you set a hostname in Raspberry Pi Imager, http://<hostname>.local/ works from most computers and phones on the same network.
  • Otherwise, look the device up in your router's list of connected devices, or see Find the IP address of your Raspberry Pi.
  • A device whose Wi-Fi isn't on a network it knows runs its own hotspot. Join it, and your phone's sign-in window opens the home page; or open http://10.42.0.1/. See Wi-Fi and the hotspot.
If the home page doesn't load

The apps accept connections only from the device, so they have no address of their own on your network. If the apps show a page saying the control app isn't answering, restart it as described in If the control app is down. If nothing loads, open Cockpit at http://<device>:9090, log in with your Raspberry Pi user account, and check the services as described in System administration. Network ports lists what the device opens. If the home page loads on a computer but times out on an Android phone, see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Places and location
docs.text: The control app's Location page records where the device is and which way its sensors face. It also sets how precisely the database stores the location. Only the administrator sees the page, because it shows exact coordinates. A device that stays in one place works without it, so use it when you move the device, turn it, or plan to share its data.

docs.title: Places and deployments
docs.text:
A place is somewhere the device has been, is, or will be. Each place has an id such as 3f9a1c2e-si, an optional description that only you see, and an optional location, its latitude and longitude. A place doesn't need a location: a device with none still counts and records its data, only without saying where. One place can hold sensors that face different ways, such as a corner with a radar looking down each street.

One place is always In use. The others are Planned, entered ahead of a move, or Used, where the device has been. Claiming a new device creates its first place, First location, with no location.

Each sensor at a place, facing one way, for one stretch of time, is a deployment. Every count and reading is stored with its deployment, so you can tell where it was taken after the device moves. Moving to another place, or turning a sensor, starts a new deployment, and the earlier ones keep what they recorded.

The exact location is kept in the control app and in Node-RED's settings file, config.yml. The database stores the place's id and the location rounded to the precision you choose.

docs.title: The Location page
docs.text:
Location is in the control app's menu, after Detection. The card at the top shows the place in use: its description, its id, the location as the database stores it, the exact location, whether the device shares its data with a ThingsBoard server, and the way each sensor faces. Then come the list of places and, last, the precision.

Each place in the list shows its description, or No description, its mark (In use, Planned, or Used), its id, and its location as the database stores it. Select a place to open it. An open place shows:

  • Imported from your previous settings for a place that came from an older version's data; see Update the software.
  • When the place was first and last used, or Not used yet.
  • How many events were recorded there, and between which dates.
  • Its deployments, newest first, grouped by when they were deployed: the sensors started together sit under one date, each with the way it faced and Correct bearing. A radar deployed with a camera is indented under it. A sensor that ended before the rest of its group says when.
  • The buttons for what you can do with the place: Deploy here for a planned place, Re-deploy here for a used one, or Modify deployment for the place in use; Edit for a planned place; Correct location for a used place or the place in use that has a location; and Delete for any place but the one in use.

Before any place was recorded counts the deployments that had already ended when the device got its first place. They belong to no place, and the database keeps them as they are. Deployments still running then joined that first place.

If Node-RED hasn't answered yet, as right after an update, a warning at the top says past places may be missing. Reload the page once Node-RED is running. Opening the control app's home page or Status page sets the places up too.

docs.title: Add a place
docs.text:
Choose Add a place, fill in what you know, and Save. The place is added as planned.

  • Description: a name for the place, such as "Front of the school". It never leaves the device.
  • Coordinates: the latitude and longitude, pasted from a maps app as one value, such as 45.52252, -122.69120. Use a dot as the decimal mark. The device keeps five decimal places, about a metre. Leave the field empty for a place with no location.
  • Which way each sensor faces here: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW, or Not set, for each sensor turned on in the settings.

Use this phone's location fills in the coordinates from your phone's location. Browsers share a location only with pages opened over HTTPS, and the device uses plain HTTP, so the form usually says to paste coordinates instead.

To change a planned place, open it and choose Edit. A place that has been used can't be edited; correct it instead.

docs.title: Move or turn the device
docs.text:
When the device moves to another place, record it from that place: Deploy here if the place is planned, or Re-deploy here if the device has been there before. When a sensor is turned to face another way, record it with Modify deployment on the place in use.

  1. Open the place, and choose its button.
  2. Check the review. For each sensor, it says whether a new deployment starts, the way the sensor faced before, and the way it faces now, which you can change. Under the sensors are what the database will store for the place and whether the device shares its data.
  3. Choose Deploy, Re-deploy, or Modify.

The page waits while Node-RED starts the new deployments, then lists their ids, each with Copy. Counts from then on belong to the new deployments.

In Modify deployment, the review starts with each sensor's bearing as it is, and each sensor reads Unchanged until you change its bearing. Modify stays off until at least one bearing changes, and only the sensors you turned start a new deployment.

Don't deploy twice

If Node-RED hasn't loaded the new settings within about 20 seconds, the page says the settings are saved and the deployments appear once Node-RED loads them. If the connection drops while the page waits, it says the settings may already be saved. In both cases, close the dialog and check the place in the list before you deploy again.

A move usually also needs the camera's zones adjusted; see First-time setup.

docs.title: Correct a wrong location or bearing
docs.text:
A correction is for a value that was entered wrong. It changes what the records already say, and starts no new deployment. If the device moved or was turned, record that instead.

  • Correct location, on a used place or the place in use, takes a new latitude and longitude. Every record from the place then says it was at the new point, rounded to the precision each was stored at. For the place in use, config.yml takes the new point too. A point more than about 1 km from the old one looks like a move, so the page asks a second time and gives the distance. A place with no location can't be corrected to one: add a new place with the location, and deploy it.
  • Correct bearing, on each deployment in an open place, takes the way the sensor really faced. Every record from that deployment then says so. For a deployment that is still running, config.yml takes the new bearing too.

Each correction can have a Reason, which is kept with the correction on the device. Copies of the database already downloaded, and data already uploaded, keep the old values.

docs.title: Import places from a file
docs.text:
To plan several places at once, choose Import places. Pick a CSV file, or paste its lines into the box.

  • The first line is the header. It starts with description,lat,lon, then has one column for each sensor turned on in the settings, named as in the settings. The dialog shows this device's header.
  • Each further line is one place. Leave lat and lon both empty for a place with no location. A sensor's column holds the way it faces, n, ne, e, se, s, sw, w, or nw, or nothing.
  • A file can be up to 64 KiB.

For a device with the Pi camera and one radar:

description,lat,lon,picam_h265,TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00
Front of the school,45.52252,-122.69120,n,n
Corner by the park,,,e,e

Choose Preview to see the places the file holds and, by line number, any lines with a problem. Import adds the places as planned. It's offered only when every line can be read, and it adds all of them or none.

docs.title: Delete a place
docs.text:
Open the place and choose Delete, then confirm. A planned place is removed from the list. A used place's exact location is deleted with it, and the database keeps the rounded location stored with each of its records. Deleting can't be undone.

The place in use can't be deleted. Deploy another place first.

docs.title: Choose the precision
docs.text:
Precision, at the end of the page, sets how much of the location the database stores. To better protect your privacy, it's rounded to about 1 km by default. The choices stay closed until you open Change the precision, which also shows the current choice, because most devices never need to change it. The setting is for the whole device, not for one place. Each choice shows how the same point would be stored:

Choice The database stores No location stored No coordinates About 10 km (45.5, -122.7) One decimal place, about a city About 1 km (45.52, -122.69), the default Two decimal places, about a neighborhood

The exact location is never stored in the database. It stays on this device, and a later update will let you choose to export the database with each place's exact location, for analysis and mapping. Choose one and Save.

  • A coarser choice applies to the deployments running now at once. Rows stored before them keep their precision unless you tick Also round the rows already stored, which asks first, because it can't be undone.
  • No location stored removes the stored location from the deployments running now at once. Tick Also remove it from the rows already stored to remove it from every row in the database as well, which also asks first. The exact location stays on the device, but the database can't get the rounded values back.
  • A finer choice applies from the next deployment. Rows already stored stay as they are, because what was rounded away can't come back.

docs.title: What leaves the device
docs.text:
• A place's description, and the reasons you give for corrections, never leave the device.
  • A copy of the database holds the place's id and its location at the stored precision: about a neighborhood at about 1 km, or about a city at about 10 km. The exact location isn't in it.
  • A correction or a coarser precision changes the device's own records only. Copies of the database already downloaded, and data already uploaded, keep the values they had.

To change these values in config.yml by hand, see Edit the location by hand.

docs.title: Cockpit
docs.text: Log in to the device as the administrator, open Cockpit from the home page, and log in again with your Raspberry Pi user account. Cockpit also answers on http://<device>:9090 with only the Raspberry Pi login, which works when the control app doesn't. Cockpit shows the services and their logs, the Podman containers, system updates, and a terminal, so most administration needs no SSH client.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
The Traffic Monitor runs as systemd services. The app containers run inside one Podman pod. nginx and the control app run on the host, outside the pod, so the home page and the login stay up when the pod is down.

Start with the control app's Status page: it shows each service's state, and when one has stopped or keeps failing, its check has a Restart button. Use Cockpit or SSH for the rest, such as restarting the control app itself, or a service that looks running but misbehaves.

Service What it runs traffic-monitor.service The pod that holds Frigate, Node-RED, and Plate Recognizer if installed frigate.service Frigate, object detection node-red-tm.service Node-RED: the Traffic Monitor logic, dashboards, database, and MQTT broker tm-control.service The control app: the home page's data, the login, the device's accounts, and the status checks. nginx asks it to check the login for every app. revproxy.service nginx, which serves the home page and the /dashboard/, /frigate/, and other paths plate-recognizer.service The optional Plate Recognizer add-on go2rtc_server.service go2rtc, which reads the Pi camera and streams it to Frigate. It runs on the host, not in the pod.

Over SSH:

sudo systemctl status traffic-monitor.service   # or any service above
sudo systemctl restart node-red-tm.service      # after editing node-red-tm.env
sudo journalctl -u frigate.service -f           # follow a service's log
sudo podman ps                                  # running containers

docs.title: When to restart what
docs.text: After you Do this Edit Node-RED's config.yml Nothing. The Traffic Monitor reads the file again when you save it. If the change doesn't show, check the file for a YAML error. For the location, use the control app's Location page instead; Edit the location by hand says what a hand edit does. Edit node-red-tm.env sudo systemctl restart node-red-tm.service. The container reads the file only when it starts. Edit frigate.env sudo systemctl restart frigate.service. Change the MQTT broker login in node-red-tm.env bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm. A restart isn't enough; Env file settings explains why. Change Frigate's config in its UI Choose Save & Restart in Frigate's config editor, or restart frigate.service. Plug in a radar Rerun the installer for Node-RED so the radar is passed to the container: bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm. Add or change an AI accelerator Rerun the installer with -t detectors -t frigate, then update Frigate's detector settings. See Add an accelerator later. See a page saying the control app isn't answering sudo systemctl restart tm-control.service, or restart it in Cockpit on port 9090. See If the control app is down. Move the device to a new site Choose Deploy here on the new place on the Location page, then adjust the zones as in First-time setup.

docs.title: The device's card
docs.text: sudo tm-control card prints the device's address, the name and password of its hotspot, and its setup code while it's unclaimed. It needs sudo because the code is in a file only root can read, and the password in a file only root and the installing user's group can. sudo tm-control card --json prints the same values as JSON. If you lose the administrator's password, sudo tm-control reset-admin starts the accounts over; see If the administrator's password is lost.

docs.title: Where things are
docs.text:
The settings and data live under /opt/traffic-monitor/.

Path Contents node-red-tm/config/config.yml Traffic Monitor settings. See config.yml settings. node-red-tm/node-red-tm.env Radar ports, database path, MQTT broker. See Env file settings. node-red-tm/db/tmdb.sqlite The database. db/backup/ holds the copy saved before the most recent schema change. After the upgrade that rounded the stored coordinates, that copy still has the exact ones, so don't share it. frigate/config/config.yml Frigate's settings, including zones and masks. frigate/config/model_cache/ The models Frigate runs, such as a Frigate+ model's two files. The control app's Detection page uploads, downloads, and deletes them. frigate/frigate.env Frigate's environment, including the Frigate+ API key, which comes from the device's secrets. See Env file settings. frigate/storage/ Frigate's snapshots and recordings. plate-recognizer/plate-recognizer.env Plate Recognizer settings, if the add-on is installed. Its token and license key come from the device's secrets, which you set on the Device page.

The control app and the installer keep a few files elsewhere. Read them, but don't edit them.

Path Contents /var/lib/tm-control/state.sqlite The control app's accounts, the license acceptance, and a log of account changes. Only the control app writes it. /etc/traffic-monitor/manifest.json What the installer installed and found, which the control app reads /etc/traffic-monitor/secrets/ Passwords and keys the installer generated on the device, including the hotspot's password, and the tokens and keys you enter on the Device page and the Detection page /etc/traffic-monitor/setup-code The setup code, until the device is claimed

docs.title: Wi-Fi and the hotspot
docs.text:
When a Traffic Monitor's Wi-Fi isn't on a network it knows, the unit runs a hotspot of its own. The hotspot is how you reach a unit at the roadside, where there's no router. It runs whether or not the unit is also on Ethernet.

The hotspot's name is TM- and four characters from the unit's serial number, such as TM-4F2A. It uses WPA2 on the 2.4 GHz band. The Status page shows its state.

docs.title: Join the hotspot
docs.text:
1. Find the hotspot's name and password on the unit's card. The card is the printout that came with a pre-built unit; for a unit you installed yourself, the installer shows it at the end of its run on the device. sudo tm-control card on the unit prints it again, together with the setup code while the unit is unclaimed.
  2. On your phone, join the hotspot with that password. Your phone may say the network has no internet. Stay connected.
  3. The phone's sign-in window opens the control app by itself, on its login or setup page. If it doesn't, open http://10.42.0.1/ in a browser. The unit's .local name, http://<hostname>.local/, also works.

The hotspot has no internet, and a phone on it reaches only the unit. Nothing on the unit's Ethernet or home network is reachable from the hotspot.

docs.title: Phones
docs.text:
• Android 17: the sign-in window is the way in. Android 17 browsers can't open the unit while the phone is on its hotspot, so don't close the window until you're done. See the Android 17 entry if the page doesn't open on your home network either.
    • The database and JSON downloads on the Data export page save from the sign-in window. The unit prepares the database twice there, once for the window and once for the phone's downloader, so the wait before a database download starts is about double.
    • Download diagnostics on the Device page doesn't save from the sign-in window: the phone says "Could not download". Download it from a computer on the unit's network instead.
    • Frigate's downloads, such as a snapshot, don't save from the sign-in window either.
  • iPhone: to stay on the hotspot and save downloads, tap Cancel on the sign-in sheet and choose Use Without Internet. Then open http://10.42.0.1/ or the unit's .local name in a browser. The login and setup pages show that name while the phone is on the hotspot. Without that choice the iPhone goes back to another network it knows, and a download in progress is cut off. The sign-in sheet itself shows a downloaded file's contents instead of saving it.

Tested with a Pixel 7 on Android 17 and with Firefox on an iPhone on iOS 18.7, in November 2026.

docs.title: When the hotspot runs
docs.text:
The hotspot yields to the networks the unit has saved. A unit joins a saved network that's in range, and the hotspot runs when none is.

Situation What happens The unit starts with a saved network in range It's on the network within a minute. The hotspot stays off. The unit starts with no saved network in range The hotspot is up about 15 seconds after the unit starts. The unit's Wi-Fi network disappears The hotspot starts about 75 seconds later. A saved network has the wrong password The hotspot is away for about a minute while the unit tries the network, then comes back.

While the hotspot is up and nobody is joined to it, the unit looks for its saved networks every 5 minutes and joins one it hears. A network that won't join is tried again about 10 minutes after the failure, then about 20 minutes after the next one, then about 65 minutes after each further failure. While a phone is joined to the hotspot, the unit doesn't look, so nothing interrupts the phone.

The Status page's Hotspot check says which of these the unit is in, and its Restart the hotspot button has the unit look at its radio at once.

Turn the hotspot off

A unit with its hotspot off has no wireless way in when its Wi-Fi network is missing. To stop the hotspot from starting by itself, run sudo nmcli connection modify tm-hotspot connection.autoconnect no. The installer leaves that setting as you set it. To turn the hotspot on again, set it to yes.

docs.title: The password
docs.text:
The installer makes the password on the unit, at random, when it sets up the hotspot. It's twelve letters and digits in three groups, such as ABCD-EFGH-JKLM, and it's different on every unit. It never comes from the serial number, so knowing the name tells nobody the password.

The unit keeps it in /etc/traffic-monitor/secrets/hotspot_password, readable only by root and the installing user's group (tmadmin unless you installed with -g). To read it, run sudo tm-control card on the unit. Over Ethernet or SSH works when you're locked out of the hotspot. The installer shows the card on the terminal and keeps the password out of its log; a run from another computer with -H prints only a reminder of the command.

docs.title: Change the password
docs.text:
1. On the unit, open the password file for editing with sudoedit /etc/traffic-monitor/secrets/hotspot_password. Replace its contents with one line of 8 to 63 characters.
  2. Run bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t wifi. The installer sets the hotspot's password to the file's.
  3. Restart the hotspot, or wait for its next start. The installer never restarts a hotspot that is up, so a phone joined to it stays joined until then. To apply the password at once, reboot the unit, or run sudo nmcli connection up tm-hotspot. Every phone on the hotspot drops, and each rejoins with the new password.

A screen in the control app for changing the password is planned.

docs.title: For sellers
docs.text:
sudo tm-control card --json prints the card's values as JSON, for a label or a packing slip:

{
  "hostname": "tm-01",
  "local_url": "http://tm-01.local/",
  "hotspot": {"name": "TM-4F2A", "password": "ABCD-EFGH-JKLM", "url": "http://10.42.0.1/"},
  "claimed": false,
  "setup_code": "ABCD-EFGH"
}

setup_code is null once the unit is claimed. The command needs sudo, and it prints to the terminal only. Nothing stores or logs the card, so don't paste the output where others can read it.

docs.title: A hotspot you set up by hand
docs.text:
A hotspot you made yourself in NetworkManager is kept. When a unit has no profile named tm-hotspot, the installer takes over your access-point profile, the one that starts by itself and was used last, renames it tm-hotspot, and stops any other access point from starting. Its name on air, password, band, and hidden setting stay as you set them. The installer sets the profile's address to 10.42.0.1 and its priority below your saved networks, and copies the password into the password file.

A hand-made hotspot with no password shows as a problem on the Status page, because anyone nearby can join it. To set a password, run these two commands on the unit, with a password of 8 to 63 characters in place of <password>:

sudo nmcli connection modify tm-hotspot 802-11-wireless-security.key-mgmt wpa-psk 802-11-wireless-security.proto rsn 802-11-wireless-security.pairwise ccmp 802-11-wireless-security.group ccmp 802-11-wireless-security.psk '<password>'
sudoedit /etc/traffic-monitor/secrets/hotspot_password

In the file, write the same password on one line. That keeps the card right, and the installer then keeps the profile's password the same as the file's. An empty file tells the installer to leave the hotspot's security alone. The new password applies when the hotspot next starts; see step 3 of Change the password.

A hotspot with a hidden name

If you hid your hand-made hotspot's name, a phone doesn't list it. On Android, choose Add network, type the name, and tick Hidden network.

docs.title: Who can see the hotspot
docs.text: A hotspot on a pole is visible to anyone passing, and public Wi-Fi maps record where names are seen. The name TM- and four characters shows that a Traffic Monitor is nearby and doesn't say where it is. The password is what keeps people out of the control app. Control app and login explains what its login protects.

docs.title: The Wi-Fi country
docs.text:
Wi-Fi rules differ by country, and a radio with no country set uses limited worldwide settings. The installer asks for the country, as a two-letter code such as US or GB, when the unit has none. Press Enter to accept US. With -y, it keeps the unit's country, or sets US when there is none. To set it without being asked, or to change it, run the installer with -w:

bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t wifi -w GB

The change applies at once, with no reboot. The Status page warns while no country is set.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A network the unit is also connected to that uses 10.42.0.x addresses clashes with the hotspot's fixed address. Give that network another range.
  • The hotspot runs on the built-in radio, wlan0. If a USB Wi-Fi adapter takes that name, the hotspot stays off, and the Status page says so. Unplug the adapter and reboot.
